blocks.text:
You can know a great deal of Java and still fumble an interview, because an interview tests something slightly different from knowledge: whether you can explain, reason aloud, and stay calm when you hit the edge of what you know. This chapter explains how Java hiring processes are usually organised, what each round is really checking, and how to answer so that the interviewer can see your thinking. The chapters after it contain 160 questions with model answers that you can use to practise.

### The shape of the process

Processes differ by company, but a Java backend or SDE hiring loop usually has the same building blocks.

rows: Data structures and algorithms under a clock, sometimes with MCQs on Java, SQL and OS
Practise timed problems; revise Big-O; know the standard library
Core Java: OOP, collections, strings, exceptions, plus one or two coding problems
The Q&A chapters in this Part, and the coding chapters that follow
Depth: concurrency, JVM and memory, your project, design of a small system
Your own project, the concurrency and JVM Parts, a few design sketches
Communication, ownership, motivation, how you handle conflict and failure
Two or three honest stories using situation, action, result
blocks.caption: Typical rounds for a fresher or early-career Java developer.

blocks.text:
Many companies merge the first two technical rounds. Product companies lean toward algorithms; service companies lean toward breadth of Java and framework vocabulary; startups lean toward "build this small thing now". Read the job description and weigh your preparation accordingly.

### What interviewers are really testing

Behind every question there is usually one of four intentions.

- **Do you have a correct mental model?** "Is Java pass-by-value?" is not a trivia question. A wrong model produces bugs, and a right one lets you predict what code does without running it.
- **Can you connect a concept to a consequence?** Knowing that `HashMap` uses `hashCode` is trivia. Knowing that a mutable key with a changing hash makes the entry unreachable is understanding.
- **Do you know the trade-off?** "ArrayList or LinkedList?" has no single answer. A good answer names the access pattern, the cost model, and the practical reality (cache locality usually wins).
- **Have you actually written code?** Follow-ups such as "what did you do in your project when that failed?" separate people who read from people who built. This is why the project chapters of this book matter: they give you real experience to quote.

### How to structure an answer

A reliable shape for a conceptual question is **definition, mechanism, example, trade-off**, delivered in 30 to 90 seconds.

1. One-sentence definition, in your own words.
2. How it works underneath (one or two sentences: this is where you stand out).
3. A tiny example or a consequence ("so if you do X, Y happens").
4. The catch or the alternative, so you show judgement.

Then stop. Interviewers will probe the part they care about. Monologues of five minutes feel safe but they hide where your understanding ends, and a clumsy tangent can open a trap you did not need to enter.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?" A weak answer lists syntax differences. A strong answer says: an interface defines a capability contract that unrelated classes can implement, and a class can implement many; an abstract class is a partially built base for a family of closely related classes, with state and constructors, and a class can extend only one. Then add the modern nuance: since Java 8 interfaces can have `default` methods, so the line is about state and identity, not about "interfaces cannot have code".

### Whiteboard and live-coding habits

- **Restate the problem** and ask about inputs: size, duplicates, nulls, sorted or not, memory limits. Interviewers often leave gaps on purpose.
- **Start with a brute force and say its complexity.** Then improve. A correct slow solution beats a half-finished clever one.
- **Talk while you think.** Silence is ambiguous; narration lets the interviewer help you.
- **Write real Java**, not pseudo-code: correct types, generics, and imports named. Use meaningful names; `i` and `j` are fine for loops, nothing else is.
- **Test with a small example by hand** before saying "done": an empty input, one element, and a typical case.
- **State complexity** in time and space, and name what dominates.
- **If you are stuck**, say what you know, what you tried, and what you would try next. "I would first check the edge case when the list has one element" is a good sentence.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Never bluff. "I am not certain, but I believe X because Y, and I would confirm in the Javadoc" is a strong answer. Confident wrong answers are remembered; honest partial answers are forgiven.

### Talking about your project

Every technical round includes "tell me about a project". Prepare a two-minute version with this skeleton: the problem, your role, the design in three sentences, the hardest bug or trade-off, and what you would change. Be ready to open the code in your head: why that collection, how errors are handled, what happens under concurrency, how you tested it. If you built one of the projects from this book, extend it (a new feature, a failure mode) so you have a genuine story.

### How to use the Q&A chapters

Each question carries a difficulty tag: **basic** (expected from everyone), **intermediate** (expected from a good candidate), **advanced** (separates strong candidates). Cover the answer, say yours aloud, then compare. The model answers are deliberately short; the chapters earlier in the book hold the full explanation, and the answers name the topic so you can go back. Code snippets in the answers were run on JDK 21 unless marked otherwise.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Interviews test models, consequences, trade-offs and real experience, not recitation.

- Answer with definition, mechanism, example, trade-off, then stop.
- Clarify, brute-force, optimise, test by hand, state complexity.
- Prepare a two-minute project story and know its weak points.
- Honest partial answers beat confident wrong ones.

sections.title: Interview Q&A: Language, OOP, Strings, Exceptions and I/O

blocks.text:
### I/O

Forty questions, in two groups. Answers are written to be spoken in under a minute. Difficulty is marked on each heading.

### Language and object-oriented Java

#### Q1. [basic] What are the JDK, JRE and JVM?

The **JVM** executes bytecode: it loads classes, manages memory with a garbage collector, and runs code through an interpreter plus a JIT compiler. The **JRE** is the JVM plus the standard class library. The **JDK** adds the development tools (`javac`, `jar`, `jshell`, `javap`, `jcmd`). Since Java 11 Oracle no longer ships a standalone JRE; you install a JDK, or use `jlink` to build a trimmed runtime.

#### Q2. [basic] Why is Java called platform independent?

The compiler produces bytecode for an abstract machine, not for a CPU. Each operating system has its own JVM that turns that bytecode into native instructions. The same `.class` file therefore runs anywhere a JVM exists. The JVM itself is platform specific; the bytecode and the language semantics (fixed sizes of `int`, `long`) are not.

#### Q3. [basic] What is the difference between == and equals()?

`==` compares primitive values, or for references whether both refer to the same object. `equals()` compares logical content, if the class overrides it; the default `Object.equals` is just `==`. Never compare strings or boxed values with `==`.

Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d) + " " + c.equals(d));

Boxing uses `Integer.valueOf`, which caches -128 to 127, so `a == b` is true by accident and `c == d` is false.

#### Q4. [basic] Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Always pass-by-value. For objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference, so the callee can mutate the object the caller sees, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller's variable.

blocks.text:
#### Q5. [basic] Primitive types versus wrapper classes. When do you use each?

There are eight primitives (`byte short int long float double char boolean`). They hold values directly, cannot be null, and are fast. Wrappers (`Integer`, `Long`, ...) are objects, needed for generics (`List<Integer>`), nullability and library APIs. Prefer primitives for arithmetic and fields that always have a value. Danger: unboxing a null throws `NullPointerException`, and boxing in tight loops allocates objects.

#### Q6. [basic] Explain final, finally and finalize.

`final` is a modifier: a final variable is assigned once, a final method cannot be overridden, a final class cannot be extended. `finally` is a block that runs after `try`/`catch` whether or not an exception occurred. `finalize()` was a pre-GC hook; it is deprecated for removal since Java 18 and must not be used. Use try-with-resources or `Cleaner` instead.

#### Q7. [basic] What is the difference between overloading and overriding?

Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists in the same class (or hierarchy); chosen at compile time by the static types of the arguments. Overriding: a subclass supplies a new body for an inherited instance method with the same signature; chosen at run time by the object's actual class (dynamic dispatch). Use `@Override` so the compiler checks you really are overriding.

#### Q8. [intermediate] Can you override a static or private method?

No. Static methods belong to the class and are *hidden*, not overridden: the method chosen depends on the declared type of the reference. Private methods are not inherited, so a same-named method in a subclass is a new, unrelated method. Fields are hidden too, never overridden.

#### Q9. [basic] Abstract class or interface?

Use an interface for a capability that unrelated types can have (`Comparable`, `Runnable`); a class can implement many. Use an abstract class for a base with shared state, constructors and partial implementation; a class extends only one. Interfaces cannot hold instance state, but since Java 8 can have `default` and `static` methods, and since 9 `private` ones.

#### Q10. [intermediate] Two interfaces provide the same default method. What happens?

The implementing class does not compile until it resolves the conflict by overriding the method. Inside it you can pick one version with `InterfaceName.super.method()`. A concrete method inherited from a class always wins over an interface default ("class wins" rule).

#### Q11. [basic] What are the four pillars of OOP?

**Encapsulation** (hide state behind methods, enforce invariants), **abstraction** (expose what, hide how), **inheritance** (reuse and specialise via a base type) and **polymorphism** (one type, many behaviours via overriding and interfaces). Be ready to give one concrete Java example of each, and to say that composition is often better than inheritance.

#### Q12. [intermediate] Composition or inheritance?

Inheritance models "is-a" and couples the subclass to the superclass's implementation: a change in the parent can break children (the fragile base class problem). Composition ("has-a") holds another object and delegates, which is easier to change and test. Rule of thumb: inherit only when the subclass truly is a specialised parent and the parent was designed for extension; otherwise compose and depend on an interface.

#### Q13. [intermediate] Why does Java not support multiple inheritance of classes?

To avoid the diamond problem (ambiguity about which inherited state and method to use) and the complexity of combining state from several parents. Java allows multiple inheritance of *type* via interfaces, and of behaviour via default methods, which have an explicit resolution rule (Q10). Multiple inheritance of *state* is deliberately absent.

**Q14. \[intermediate\] In what order are fields, blocks and constructors initialised? What is the trap?** Class loading first: static fields and static blocks, once, in textual order. Per `new`: the superclass constructor runs first (itself initialising its fields, then its body), then the subclass's field initialisers and instance blocks, then the subclass constructor body. The trap: if a superclass constructor calls an overridable method, the subclass override runs before the subclass fields are initialised, so it sees defaults.

Never call overridable methods from constructors; make them `final` or private if you must.

**Q15. \[intermediate\] What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what breaks if you violate it?** Equal objects must have equal hash codes; `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and `x.equals(null)` is false. Hash-based collections find a bucket with `hashCode` and then confirm with `equals`. If you override only `equals`, two equal objects usually land in different buckets and `contains` misses them.

The result is *typically* false, not guaranteed; that is what makes the bug nasty. Override both, based on the same fields, or use a `record`.

#### Q16. [intermediate] How do you build an immutable class?

Declare the class `final` (or make constructors private), make all fields `private final`, set them in the constructor, provide no setters, and defensively copy any mutable inputs and outputs (arrays, `Date`, collections; use `List.copyOf`). Immutable objects are thread-safe by construction, safe as map keys and easy to reason about. A `record` gives most of this for free, but is only *shallowly* immutable: a `List` component is still mutable unless you copy it.

#### Q17. [basic] What are the access modifiers?

`private` (same class), package-private (no keyword; same package), `protected` (same package plus subclasses), `public` (everywhere). With modules (Java 9) a package must also be `exports`-ed for outside access. Default to the narrowest access that works.

#### Q18. [intermediate] What kinds of nested classes exist?

A **static nested** class has no reference to an outer instance. An **inner** (non-static) class holds a hidden reference to its enclosing instance, which can keep the outer object alive (a classic leak) and complicates serialization. A **local** class is declared in a method. An **anonymous** class is a one-off subclass or implementation; lambdas replace most uses for functional interfaces. Prefer static nested unless you need the outer instance.

#### Q19. [basic] What is special about enums?

An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances, created once by the JVM. It can have fields, constructors, methods and per-constant bodies, and implement interfaces. They are type-safe, work in `switch`, are singletons per constant, and serialize safely by name. Use `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` for compact, fast collections keyed by enum.

#### Q20. [intermediate] What is a record and when do you not use one?

A record (Java 16) is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier: the compiler generates the canonical constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. Use it for DTOs, map keys, return tuples. Do not use it for entities with identity and lifecycle, classes that need mutable state, or inheritance (records are final and cannot extend a class).

#### Q21. [intermediate] Shallow copy versus deep copy; is clone() a good idea?

A shallow copy copies references, so the copy and original share inner objects; a deep copy duplicates the whole object graph. `Object.clone()` does a shallow field copy, requires `Cloneable`, bypasses constructors and is widely considered broken (Effective Java). Prefer a copy constructor or static factory, and copy mutable parts explicitly.

#### Q22. [intermediate] Which numeric traps appear most often?

Integer overflow wraps silently; compound assignment hides a cast; `char` arithmetic gives `int`; ternary operands undergo numeric promotion; floating point is binary. Run this to see them:

System.out.println((char) ('a' + 1));            // cast back to char

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2")));

Use `Math.addExact` to fail on overflow, `BigDecimal` (built from strings) for money, and never compare floating-point values with `==`.

### Strings, exceptions and I/O

#### Q23. [basic] Why is String immutable?

Immutability makes strings safe to share (the string pool), safe as `HashMap` keys (the hash can be cached), thread-safe without locks, and secure (a path or class name cannot change after validation). The cost is that every modification creates a new object; use `StringBuilder` for repeated edits.

#### Q24. [basic] What is the string pool? What does new String("x") do?

Literals and compile-time constants are interned in a pool (on the heap since Java 7), so identical literals share one object. `new String("x")` always creates a new object, distinct from the pooled one; `intern()` returns the pooled instance.

System.out.println((x == y) + " " + (x == z) + " " + (x == z.intern()));

#### Q25. [basic] String, StringBuilder or StringBuffer?

`String` is immutable. `StringBuilder` is a mutable, unsynchronized buffer: the default choice for building text in a loop. `StringBuffer` is the synchronized legacy version; you almost never need it because a builder is rarely shared across threads. A single `a + b + c` expression is fine (the compiler uses `invokedynamic`); concatenating inside a loop creates a new string per iteration, so use a builder there.

#### Q26. [advanced] Which of these is true: "a"+"b" == "ab", and the same with a variable?

Compile-time constants are folded and pooled, so `"a" + "b" == "ab"` is true, and so is a concatenation of `final` variables initialised with constants. A concatenation involving a non-final variable is computed at run time and creates a new object.

#### Q27. [intermediate] A common split surprise?

`String.split` takes a regex and drops *trailing* empty strings. `"a,b,,".split(",")` has length 2, not 4. Pass a negative limit (`split(",", -1)`) to keep them. Regex metacharacters must be escaped: `split("\\.")`, not `split(".")`.

#### Q28. [basic] Checked versus unchecked exceptions?

Checked exceptions (subclasses of `Exception` other than `RuntimeException`) must be caught or declared; the compiler enforces it. They model recoverable conditions outside the caller's control, such as `IOException`. Unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException` and `Error` subclasses) need no declaration and usually signal programming errors (`NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`). Modern libraries and frameworks (Spring) favour unchecked exceptions because checked ones leak through lambdas and layers.

#### Q29. [basic] Exception versus Error?

Both extend `Throwable`. `Exception` is for conditions an application may handle. `Error` signals JVM-level failures (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`, `NoClassDefFoundError`); catching them is almost always wrong, because the program state may be unsound. At most, log and shut down.

#### Q30. [intermediate] How does try-with-resources work, and what are suppressed exceptions?

Any `AutoCloseable` declared in the header is closed automatically, in *reverse* order, whether the body succeeds or throws. If the body throws and `close()` throws too, the body's exception is the one propagated and the close exceptions are attached with `addSuppressed` (read them via `getSuppressed()`).

#### Q31. [intermediate] What does return inside finally do?

A `finally` block always runs (barring `System.exit` or a JVM crash). If it contains `return`, that value replaces any pending return or exception, and the exception is silently lost. `try { return 1; } finally { return 2; }` returns 2. Never return, break or throw from `finally`.

#### Q32. [intermediate] How should you design and throw your own exceptions?

Pick checked only if callers can realistically recover; otherwise extend `RuntimeException`. Name it after the problem (`InsufficientFundsException`), include useful context fields, and always pass the original as the `cause` so the stack trace chain is kept: `new ServiceException("load failed", e)`. Do not use exceptions for normal control flow and do not catch and swallow silently. Log or rethrow, not both.

#### Q33. [basic] throw versus throws; catch ordering and multi-catch?

`throw` raises an exception object; `throws` declares what a method may throw. Catch blocks are tried in order, so a subclass catch must come before its superclass (otherwise it does not compile). Multi-catch `catch (IOException |` `SQLException e)` handles unrelated types in one block; the alternatives cannot be related by inheritance.

**Q34. \[intermediate\] How does Java serialization work? What do transient and serialVersionUID do?** A class implementing `Serializable` can be written by `ObjectOutputStream`, which walks the object graph and writes non-static, non-transient fields. `transient` fields are skipped and get default values on read (null, 0). Static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so they are not written. `serialVersionUID` identifies the class version; declare it explicitly so harmless changes do not break old data. Native serialization is fragile and a known security risk (deserialization attacks); prefer JSON or Protobuf and never deserialize untrusted data.

#### Q35. [intermediate] Byte streams versus character streams; why specify a charset?

`InputStream`/`OutputStream` move raw bytes; `Reader`/`Writer` decode bytes to characters using a charset. Always pass the charset explicitly (`StandardCharsets.UTF_8`), because the platform default differed between machines before Java 18, which made files unreadable elsewhere. Since JDK 18 (JEP 400) the default is UTF-8, but explicit is still clearer. Wrap sources in `BufferedReader`/`BufferedWriter` to avoid one system call per byte.

#### Q36. [intermediate] java.io.File or java.nio.file?

Prefer NIO.2 (`Path`, `Files`): it has real error reporting through exceptions (`File.delete` just returns false), symbolic link and attribute support, directory walking, and one-liners such as `Files.readString` and `Files.lines`. `Files.lines` and `Files.list` return streams that hold an open file, so use them in try-with-resources.

#### Q37. [basic] Which runtime exceptions do you meet most?

`NullPointerException` (use of null; helpful messages since Java 14 name the null variable), `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException`, `ClassCastException` (bad downcast), `ArithmeticException` (integer divide by zero), `NumberFormatException` (bad `parseInt` input), `ConcurrentModificationException` and `ArrayStoreException` (an `Object[]` that is really a `String[]`). Knowing each cause is a quick win.

#### Q38. [advanced] ClassNotFoundException versus NoClassDefFoundError?

`ClassNotFoundException` is a checked exception thrown when code asks for a class by name (`Class.forName`, a classloader) and it is not found. `NoClassDefFoundError` is an `Error`: the class was present at compile time but is missing, or failed static initialisation, at run time. A failed static initialiser first throws `ExceptionInInitializerError`, and later uses of the class give `NoClassDefFoundError`.

#### Q39. [advanced] Can you catch StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError?

Syntactically yes. `StackOverflowError` can sometimes be survived (the stack unwinds and you lose only that call), but deep recursion should be turned into iteration. `OutOfMemoryError` is rarely recoverable, since other threads may also fail to allocate; you can catch it to log or release a big cache, but the sane response is to fix memory use or let the process die and restart. Do not use these for control flow.

#### Q40. [advanced] How does Java choose among overloaded methods?

In three phases: first by subtyping and widening only (no boxing, no varargs); then with boxing/unboxing; then varargs. Within a phase, the most specific method wins. So `g(5)` with `g(long)`, `g(Integer)` and `g(int...)` calls `g(long)` (widening beats boxing). `f(null)` with `f(Object)` and `f(String)` picks `String` as the more specific type. The choice uses the *static* type: `Object o = "s"; f(o)` calls `f(Object)`.

blocks.text: "Why should you override `hashCode` whenever you override `equals`?" Because `HashMap`, `HashSet` and friends use `hashCode` to choose a bucket and only then call `equals`. Equal objects with different hash codes are searched for in the wrong bucket and are not found. State the contract (equal objects have equal hashes; unequal ones may collide), mention that the fields used in both must match, and add that mutating a key field after insertion loses the entry.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring applications the same ideas appear as: `@Entity` classes with careful `equals`/`hashCode` (often on a business key, not the generated id), DTOs as records, custom runtime exceptions mapped to HTTP statuses by `@ControllerAdvice`, and try-with-resources for JDBC connections and streams.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The Java core language is a set of consistent rules; interviews probe whether you can apply them.

- Java is pass-by-value; reference values are copies of pointers.
- Overloading is compile-time, overriding is run-time; fields and statics are hidden, not overridden.
- Override `equals` and `hashCode` together, prefer immutability and records for value types.
- Strings are immutable and pooled; compile-time constants fold, run-time concatenation does not.
- Prefer try-with-resources, wrap with cause, never swallow or return from `finally`.

sections.title: Interview Q&A: Collections, Generics, Streams and Functional Java

blocks.text:
### Functional Java

Forty more questions. The collections questions are the most reliably asked in Java interviews of any level, usually in the form "how does HashMap work" followed by a chain of follow-ups. Read the answers, then explain them aloud with a drawing.

### Collections and generics

#### Q41. [basic] Describe the Collections Framework hierarchy.

`Iterable` is the root of `Collection`, which splits into `List` (ordered, indexed, duplicates allowed), `Set` (no duplicates) and `Queue`/`Deque` (head and tail operations). `Map` is *not* a `Collection`; it maps keys to values and exposes `keySet()`, `values()` and `entrySet()` views. Main implementations: `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, `TreeSet`, `ArrayDeque`, `PriorityQueue`, `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap`. Always declare variables by the interface (`List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>()`).

#### Q42. [basic] ArrayList or LinkedList?

`ArrayList` is a resizable array: `get(i)` is O(1), append is amortised O(1), insert or remove in the middle is O(n) because of shifting (a very fast `System.arraycopy`). `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list: insert/remove at a known node is O(1), but `get(i)` is O(n) and every element is a separate node object, which is bad for memory and CPU caches. In practice `ArrayList` wins almost always; for a queue or stack use `ArrayDeque`.

#### Q43. [intermediate] How does ArrayList grow?

It keeps an `Object[]`. The no-arg constructor starts with an empty shared array and allocates capacity 10 on the first `add`. When full it allocates a new array of about 1.5 times the size (`oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)`) and copies. If you know the final size, use `new ArrayList<>(n)` to avoid repeated copying. `trimToSize()` releases unused slots.

#### Q44. [basic] How does HashMap work internally?

It holds an array of buckets (default capacity 16, load factor 0.75). `put(k, v)` computes `hash = h ^ (h >>> 16)` from `k.hashCode()` to mix high bits into low bits, picks the bucket `(n - 1) & hash` (n is always a power of two), and walks the chain in that bucket comparing hashes and then `equals`. If the key exists the value is replaced; otherwise a node is appended. When `size` exceeds `capacity * 0.75`, the table doubles and entries are redistributed (each entry stays in the same bucket or moves by exactly the old capacity). Average `get`/`put` is O(1).

#### Q45. [advanced] What changed in Java 8 for HashMap collisions?

A bucket chain with at least 8 nodes, in a table of at least 64 buckets, is converted into a red-black tree (lookup O(log n) instead of O(n)); smaller tables resize instead. A tree shrinks back to a list at 6 nodes or fewer. This protects against poor hash functions and hash-flooding attacks. Tree nodes order by hash, then by `Comparable` if the key class implements it, so comparable keys behave better under collision. **Q46. \[intermediate\] HashMap, Hashtable, Collections.synchronizedMap and ConcurrentHashMap?** `HashMap` is unsynchronized, allows one null key and null values. `Hashtable` is legacy: every method is synchronized on one lock and no nulls are allowed. `synchronizedMap` wraps a map with one lock; iteration still needs manual locking. `ConcurrentHashMap` allows concurrent reads and fine-grained concurrent writes (CAS and per-bin locking), offers atomic operations such as `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`, and does not allow null keys or values. Use it for shared mutable maps. Part 8 covers the details.

#### Q47. [basic] How does HashSet ensure uniqueness?

A `HashSet` is a `HashMap` in disguise: elements are keys, and every key maps to one shared dummy value. `add` returns false when the key already exists, decided by `hashCode` then `equals`. `LinkedHashSet` keeps insertion order; `TreeSet` keeps sorted order and uses `compareTo`/`Comparator` instead of `equals`.

#### Q48. [intermediate] What happens if a key is mutated after insertion?

The entry sits in the bucket for the *old* hash. Looking up the mutated key hashes to a different bucket and misses; looking up an equal copy of the old value finds the bucket but fails `equals` against the changed key. The entry is effectively lost and leaks. Use immutable keys.

#### Q49. [intermediate] Comparable versus Comparator?

`Comparable<T>` gives a class one natural ordering via `compareTo` (strings, numbers, dates). `Comparator<T>` is an external ordering, so you can sort the same class several ways without changing it. Build comparators with `Comparator.comparing(...)`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`, `nullsFirst`. The ordering must be consistent with `equals` when used in `TreeSet`/`TreeMap`, because those use compare results as equality (`compare == 0` means duplicate).

#### Q50. [intermediate] How do you build an LRU cache in Java?

Extend `LinkedHashMap` with access order enabled (third constructor argument `true`) and override `removeEldestEntry`. Every `get` moves the entry to the tail; the head is the least recently used and is evicted when the size limit is exceeded. It is not thread-safe; wrap it with a lock for concurrent use.

blocks.title: LRU with LinkedHashMap

blocks.text:
Key 2 was the least recently used, so it was evicted.

#### Q51. [intermediate] What is ConcurrentModificationException? Is it only about threads?

Fail-fast iterators of `ArrayList`, `HashMap` and others compare a `modCount` snapshot with the collection's count on each `next()`. Structural modification during iteration (other than through the iterator's own `remove`) makes the next call throw. It happens in single-threaded code too. It is best-effort, not guaranteed: removing the second-to-last element ends the loop silently because `hasNext()` returns false first.

blocks.title: Remove inside a for-each loop
Output (the first loop throws ConcurrentModificationException, shown here caught)

blocks.text:
Fixes: `Iterator.remove()`, `removeIf(predicate)`, or collect into a new list. Concurrent collections (`CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `ConcurrentHashMap`) have weakly consistent iterators that never throw it.

#### Q52. [basic] What is the trap in List.remove?

`remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)` are overloads. On a `List<Integer>`, `list.remove(1)` removes the element at index 1, while `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` removes the value 1.

#### Q53. [intermediate] List.of, Arrays.asList and Collections.unmodifiableList?

`List.of` (Java 9) is truly immutable, rejects nulls, and any mutation throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. `Arrays.asList` is a fixed-size view over the array: `set` works and writes through to the array, but `add`/`remove` throw. `Collections.unmodifiableList` is a read-only *view*: it blocks changes through the wrapper but reflects changes made to the underlying list. `List.copyOf` makes an independent immutable copy.

blocks.title: Three flavours of "unmodifiable"

blocks.text:
#### Q54. [intermediate] Which maps accept null keys?

`HashMap` and `LinkedHashMap` allow one null key and null values. `TreeMap` throws `NullPointerException` for a null key (it must compare) when using natural ordering. `ConcurrentHashMap`, `Hashtable` and the `Map.of` family reject nulls. The concurrent ban exists so that "get returned null" unambiguously means "absent".

#### Q55. [intermediate] How does PriorityQueue work, and what does iterating it show?

It is a binary min-heap stored in an array; `offer` and `poll` are O(log n), `peek` is O(1). Only the head is guaranteed to be the smallest. The array order, and therefore `toString` and iteration, is *not* sorted. To get sorted output, `poll` repeatedly. For a max-heap supply `Comparator.reverseOrder()`.

blocks.code:
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 4, 2, 3));
System.out.println(pq + " " + pq.poll() + " " + pq.peek());
blocks.title: Heap order is not sorted order

blocks.text:
#### Q56. [basic] Which class do you use as a stack or a queue?

`ArrayDeque`: `push`/`pop`/`peek` for a stack, `offer`/`poll` for a queue. It is faster than `LinkedList` and `Stack`. `Stack` and `Vector` are legacy synchronized classes. `ArrayDeque` does not allow nulls. For thread-handoff use `BlockingQueue` implementations.

#### Q57. [intermediate] Which sorting algorithm does Java use, and is it stable?

`Collections.sort`/`List.sort`/`Arrays.sort(Object[])` use TimSort (a merge sort and insertion sort hybrid): stable, O(n log n) worst case, close to O(n) on nearly sorted data. `Arrays.sort` on primitive arrays uses dual-pivot quicksort: not stable (stability is meaningless for primitives), average O(n log n). Stability matters when sorting by one key after another.

#### Q58. [advanced] When would you use EnumMap, IdentityHashMap or WeakHashMap?

`EnumMap` is an array indexed by enum ordinal: fastest and smallest map for enum keys. `IdentityHashMap` compares keys with `==`, useful for graph traversal bookkeeping and serializers. `WeakHashMap` holds keys weakly, so an entry disappears once the key is otherwise unreachable; handy for canonicalising caches, but values must not strongly reference their key or the entry never goes.

#### Q59. [intermediate] What are sequenced collections (Java 21)?

Java 21 added `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet` and `SequencedMap` for types with a defined encounter order. They give uniform `getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `addFirst`, `removeLast` and `reversed()` on `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet`, `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeSet`. Before 21, getting the last element of a `List` was `list.get(list.size() - 1)`, and of a `LinkedHashSet` required iterating. `HashSet`/`HashMap` are not sequenced.

#### Q60. [intermediate] What is type erasure?

Generics are a compile-time feature. The compiler checks types, inserts casts, and erases type parameters to their bounds (`Object` if unbounded) in the bytecode. At run time `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class. Consequences: no `new T()`, no `instanceof List<String>`, no generic arrays, no overloads that differ only in type arguments. Erasure kept Java 5 code compatible with older libraries.

blocks.code:
List<String> ls = new ArrayList<>(); List<Integer> li = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(ls.getClass() == li.getClass());
blocks.title: Same class at run time

blocks.code: true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### Q61. [advanced] Explain ? extends, ? super and PECS.

Generics are invariant: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`. Wildcards add flexibility. **Producer Extends,** **Consumer Super**: if a parameter only *produces* values you read, use `? extends T`; if it only *consumes* values you write, use `? super T`.

blocks.title: PECS

blocks.text:
You cannot add to a `List<? extends Number>` (the real element type is unknown), nor safely read specific types from `?` `super`. `Collections.copy(dest, src)` has exactly this signature.

#### Q62. [advanced] What is heap pollution, and why are raw types discouraged?

A raw type (`List` without arguments) turns off generic checking. You can add an `Integer` to what is really a `List<String>`; the compiler only warns, and the failure appears later as a `ClassCastException` at an innocent-looking `String x = list.get(0)`. Avoid raw types, and treat unchecked warnings as bugs. Generic varargs (`T...`) can pollute the heap as well; `@SafeVarargs` is only for methods that do not write into the array.

#### Q63. [intermediate] How do you write a generic method with a bound?

Put the type parameter before the return type, and bound it for the operations you need.

blocks.title: Bounded generic method

blocks.text:
`Comparable<T>` as a bound lets you call `compareTo` on the elements. Many libraries use the more permissive `<T` `extends Comparable<? super T>>`.

#### Q64. [advanced] Why can't you create new T[] or use primitives as type arguments?

Because of erasure, `T` is unknown at run time, so arrays (which are reified and check element type at run time) cannot be created for it; use `(T[]) new Object[n]` with care, or `List<T>`. Type arguments must be reference types because erased code uses `Object`; `List<int>` is not allowed (boxing to `Integer` is used, with its cost). Project Valhalla aims at changing this, but it is not part of the current LTS.

### Streams and functional Java

#### Q65. [basic] What is a stream, and how is it different from a collection?

A stream is a one-shot, lazy pipeline over a data source: source, zero or more *intermediate* operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`), and one *terminal* operation (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`) that triggers execution. A collection stores data; a stream does not store, it describes computation. Streams do not modify their source and can be consumed only once.

#### Q66. [intermediate] What does "lazy" mean here? Show it.

Intermediate operations only record steps. Nothing runs until the terminal operation, and elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline (vertical processing), so short-circuiting operations such as `limit` or `findFirst` stop early.

blocks.title: Laziness and short-circuit

blocks.code:
built
peek 1
got 1
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Nothing printed while building; only element 1 was ever pulled.

#### Q67. [basic] map versus flatMap?

`map` transforms each element into exactly one output element. `flatMap` takes a function returning a stream per element and flattens all those streams into one: use it for "one-to-many" such as lines to words, or orders to line items. Think `Stream<List<X>>` to `Stream<X>`. On `Optional`, `flatMap` avoids `Optional<Optional<T>>`.

#### Q68. [intermediate] Show groupingBy and partitioningBy.

`groupingBy(classifier)` builds a `Map<K, List<T>>`; a downstream collector (`counting`, `averagingInt`, `mapping`, `summingInt`) reduces each group; a third argument selects the map type. `partitioningBy(predicate)` always yields exactly two keys, `false` and `true`.

blocks.title: Collectors

blocks.text:
#### Q69. [intermediate] What goes wrong with Collectors.toMap?

Two elements with the same key make `toMap` throw `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key a (attempted merging` `values 1 and 1)`. Supply a merge function as the third argument (`(x, y) -> x`) and, if you need ordering, a map supplier as the fourth. A null value also throws `NullPointerException`.

#### Q70. [basic] Can you reuse a stream?

No. After a terminal operation it is consumed, and a second operation throws `IllegalStateException: stream has` `already been operated upon or closed`. Create a new stream from the source, or keep a `Supplier<Stream<T>>`.

#### Q71. [intermediate] Stream.toList() or Collectors.toList()?

`Stream.toList()` (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list and permits nulls. `Collectors.toList()` returns a `List` whose mutability and type are unspecified (today an `ArrayList`), so do not depend on it. Use `toList()` by default; use `Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)` when you need a mutable one.

#### Q72. [intermediate] When is a parallel stream a bad idea?

Parallel streams split the source and run on the common `ForkJoinPool`. They pay off for large data, CPU-bound, stateless, associative operations on easily splittable sources (arrays, `ArrayList`, ranges). They hurt with small data, I/O or blocking calls (starving the shared pool), `LinkedList` or `Stream.iterate` sources, and *shared mutable state*: `list.add` from a parallel `forEach` loses elements or throws. Measure before using. Ordered terminals such as `forEach` lose ordering; `forEachOrdered` keeps it at a cost.

#### Q73. [basic] How should you use Optional?

It is a return type that says "there may be no value". Use `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow`, `ifPresent` rather than `isPresent()` plus `get()`. Do not use it for fields, method parameters or collections (return an empty collection). `orElse(expensive())` always evaluates its argument; `orElseGet(() -> expensive())` is lazy.

blocks.code:
Optional<String> o = Optional.empty();
System.out.println(o.map(String::length).orElse(-1));
blocks.title: Optional chaining

blocks.text:
#### Q74. [basic] Name the core functional interfaces.

`Function<T,R>` (T to R), `Predicate<T>` (T to boolean), `Consumer<T>` (T to nothing), `Supplier<T>` (nothing to T), `UnaryOperator<T>`, `BinaryOperator<T>`, `BiFunction<T,U,R>`, plus primitive forms (`IntPredicate`, `ToIntFunction`) that avoid boxing. A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; `@FunctionalInterface` makes the compiler check it. `Function` composes with `andThen` and `compose`, `Predicate` with `and`, `or`, `negate`.

blocks.code:
Function<Integer, Integer> f = x -> x + 1, g = x -> x * 2;
System.out.println(f.andThen(g).apply(3) + " " + f.compose(g).apply(3));
blocks.title: Composition order

blocks.text:
`f.andThen(g)` runs f first: `(3+1)*2 = 8`. `f.compose(g)` runs g first: `3*2+1 = 7`.

#### Q75. [intermediate] Lambda versus anonymous inner class?

A lambda is compiled to an `invokedynamic` call site bootstrapped by `LambdaMetafactory`; no extra `.class` file is generated at compile time and the JVM spins the implementation at first use. An anonymous class is a real class file with its own `this`. Inside a lambda `this` means the enclosing instance, inside an anonymous class it means the anonymous object. Lambdas work only for functional interfaces; anonymous classes can implement interfaces with many methods or extend a class and hold state.

#### Q76. [intermediate] Why must captured local variables be effectively final?

A lambda can outlive the method and run on another thread, and locals live on a stack frame that will be gone. Java therefore copies the value and requires that it never changes, so copy and original cannot disagree. The usual escape hatch is a one-element array or an `AtomicInteger`, but that is a signal to restructure (for example with `reduce` or a collector). Fields are not captured by value; they are read through `this` and can change.

blocks.title: The array trick, and why not to rely on it

blocks.text:
#### Q77. [intermediate] What are the four kinds of method reference?

Static (`Integer::parseInt`), bound instance (`System.out::println`, the receiver is fixed), unbound instance (`String::length`, the first argument is the receiver), and constructor (`ArrayList::new`). A reference is just a shorter lambda; choose it when it reads better.

#### Q78. [intermediate] Build a multi-key sort.

Chain comparators and name the key extractor so the intent is obvious.

blocks.title: Comparator chain

blocks.code: [c, a, b]
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
City X first (c is older than a, so it comes first), then Y.

#### Q79. [advanced] Which stream operations are stateful, and what is their cost?

`sorted` must see every element before emitting the first; `distinct` and `limit`/`skip` (on ordered streams) keep state. A pipeline with `sorted` cannot stream a huge source in constant memory. Prefer filtering before sorting, and `IntStream`/`LongStream`/`DoubleStream` for numeric work to avoid boxing: `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).sum()` allocates no `Integer` objects.

#### Q80. [advanced] Why avoid side effects in stream operations?

Lambdas in `map`, `filter` and friends should be pure: no mutation of outside state. Side effects break under parallelism, depend on evaluation order that the spec does not promise (for example, `peek` may be skipped if the terminal operation can compute the result without it, such as `count()` on a sized source), and make code hard to read. Use `collect` or `reduce` to accumulate instead of `forEach` plus an outside list. Reserve `peek` for debugging.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Explain how HashMap handles collisions and what happens when it gets full." Hash spreading chooses a bucket; nodes with the same bucket form a linked list; once a bucket has 8 or more nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets it becomes a red-black tree, and it reverts at 6. "Full" means exceeding capacity times load factor (0.75): the table doubles, and entries are redistributed with one bit test each. Mention that a good `hashCode` and immutable keys keep operations O(1) on average, and that a pre-sized map (`new HashMap<>(expected / 0.75 + 1)`, or `HashMap.newHashMap(n)` since Java 19) avoids rehashing.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Data repositories return `Optional<T>` and `Stream<T>` (which must be closed). Controllers map entities to records with streams, group report rows with `groupingBy`, and cache with `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` or Caffeine, whose eviction policy is an improved LRU.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Collections questions are about mechanics; streams questions are about laziness and purity.

- Pick `ArrayList`, `HashMap`, `ArrayDeque` by default; know why `LinkedList` rarely wins.
- HashMap: spread hash, power-of-two table, load factor 0.75, treeify at 8 (table 64+), untreeify at 6.
- Keys must be immutable with consistent `equals`/`hashCode`; fail-fast iterators throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.
- Generics are compile-time only (erasure); use PECS for wildcards.
- Streams are lazy, single-use and should be side-effect free; collect rather than mutate.

sections.title: Interview Q&A: Concurrency, the Memory Model and the JVM

blocks.text:
### the JVM

Concurrency and JVM internals are where interviews separate candidates, because the answers cannot be memorised from syntax: they require a mental model. The forty questions below use experiments run on JDK 21. Where a result depends on timing it is marked typical.

### Concurrency and the Java Memory Model

#### Q81. [basic] Process versus thread?

A process is an isolated program instance with its own address space. Threads are execution paths inside a process that share its heap and open resources but have their own stack and program counter. Sharing makes communication cheap and bugs easy: shared mutable state needs synchronisation.

#### Q82. [basic] How can you create a thread? Runnable versus Callable?

Implement `Runnable` (or pass a lambda) to a `Thread`, subclass `Thread` (rarely good), or, best, submit tasks to an `ExecutorService`. `Runnable.run()` returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions; `Callable<V>.call()` returns a value and may throw, and is submitted to an executor, which returns a `Future<V>`. Separate the task from how it is run.

#### Q83. [basic] start() versus run()?

`start()` asks the JVM to create a new thread, which then calls `run()`. Calling `run()` directly just executes the method on the current thread; no concurrency. Calling `start()` twice throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

#### Q84. [intermediate] List the thread states.

`NEW` (created, not started), `RUNNABLE` (running or ready; includes blocked in native I/O), `BLOCKED` (waiting to enter a `synchronized` block), `WAITING` (`wait()`, `join()`, `park()` with no timeout), `TIMED_WAITING` (`sleep`, timed `wait`/`join`), `TERMINATED`.

blocks.title: Observing states

blocks.code:
NEW
TIMED_WAITING
TERMINATED
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### Q85. [basic] What does synchronized do? What is locked?

It acquires the *monitor* of an object, giving mutual exclusion and also memory visibility (release flushes, acquire sees earlier writes). On an instance method the lock is `this`; on a static method it is the `Class` object; on a block it is the object you name. Two threads using *different* lock objects do not exclude each other. The bytecode uses `monitorenter` and `monitorexit` (the latter on both normal and exceptional exits).

#### Q86. [intermediate] What does volatile guarantee and not guarantee?

It guarantees visibility (a write is seen by subsequent reads in other threads) and ordering (no reordering across the volatile access: a write happens-before a later read of the same variable). It does **not** make compound actions atomic: `count++` is read, add, write.

#### Q87. [intermediate] Demonstrate a race condition and the fixes.

Two threads each increment four counters 100,000 times.

blocks.title: Four counters, two threads

blocks.code:
vol  : below 200000
sync : 200000
atomic: 200000
blocks.title: Result after both threads join (typical; plain and vol are racy, so their totals vary)

blocks.text:
In the run on the build machine `vol` lost updates, while `plain` happened to reach 200000: a race may stay hidden, which is exactly why you reason from the memory model rather than from tests. Fixes: `synchronized`, a lock, `AtomicInteger`/`LongAdder` (lock-free CAS), or avoid sharing.

#### Q88. [advanced] What is the Java Memory Model and "happens-before"?

The JMM defines when a write by one thread is guaranteed visible to another. Without ordering, compilers and CPUs may reorder and cache. *Happens-before* edges create guarantees: program order within a thread; unlock of a monitor before every later lock of it; volatile write before every later volatile read; `Thread.start()` before the started thread's actions; a thread's actions before `join()` returns; writes to a `final` field in a constructor are visible once the reference is safely published. If there is no happens-before between a write and a read, it is a data race.

#### Q89. [intermediate] wait/notify versus sleep versus join?

`sleep(ms)` pauses the current thread and keeps any locks. `wait()` must be called while holding the object's monitor, releases it, and waits until `notify`/`notifyAll` (always inside a `while` loop re-checking the condition, because of spurious wakeups). `join()` waits for another thread to finish. Prefer higher-level tools: `BlockingQueue`, `CountDownLatch`, `Condition`.

#### Q90. [intermediate] What is a deadlock? How do you prevent it?

Threads wait on each other's locks forever. Four conditions hold together: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break one: acquire locks in a global order (breaks circular wait), use `tryLock` with timeout, hold fewer locks, or use higher-level structures. Diagnose with `jstack <pid>`, `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` (both print "Found one Java-level deadlock") or `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`.

blocks.code:
Thread d1 = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (l1) { sleep(100); synchronized (l2) { } } });
Thread d2 = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (l2) { sleep(100); synchronized (l1) { } } });

blocks.code:

deadlocked=2
blocks.title: Output after 400 ms: both threads BLOCKED; findDeadlockedThreads() reports 2

blocks.text:
#### Q91. [intermediate] synchronized versus ReentrantLock?

Both are reentrant mutexes. `ReentrantLock` adds `tryLock()` (with timeout), interruptible acquisition, optional fairness, multiple `Condition`s, and `ReadWriteLock` variants; you must `unlock()` in `finally`. `synchronized` is simpler, cannot leak a lock, and has been heavily optimised. Use `synchronized` unless you need those features.

#### Q92. [intermediate] Explain ThreadPoolExecutor parameters. Why is

#### Executors.newFixedThreadPool risky?

Parameters: core size, max size, keep-alive, work queue, thread factory, rejection policy. Behaviour: tasks go to new threads up to core size; then into the queue; only when the queue is full are threads added up to max; when both are full the handler rejects. `newFixedThreadPool` uses an *unbounded* queue, so a producer outrunning consumers eats memory until `OutOfMemoryError`; `newCachedThreadPool` can create unbounded threads. In production, construct a pool with a bounded queue and a deliberate rejection policy, and name your threads. Always `shutdown()`.

**Q93. \[intermediate\] How do exceptions in tasks reach the caller? What is CompletableFuture for?** `Future.get()` rethrows a task's exception wrapped in `ExecutionException`; if you never call `get`, the failure is silent. `CompletableFuture` composes asynchronous stages without blocking: `supplyAsync`, `thenApply`, `thenCompose` (flatMap), `thenCombine`, `allOf`, `exceptionally`, `handle`. By default async stages run on the common `ForkJoinPool`; pass your own executor for blocking work.

#### Q94. [intermediate] How do ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList work?

`ConcurrentHashMap` (since Java 8) uses lock-free reads, CAS to insert into an empty bin and a lock on the first node of a bin for other writes, so writers on different bins do not contend. Size is computed from striped counters. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` copies the whole array on each write and gives iterators a snapshot: excellent for read-mostly listener lists, terrible for write-heavy use. Neither supports a compound check-then-act across calls; use `computeIfAbsent` or `merge`.

#### Q95. [intermediate] When do you use CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore?

`CountDownLatch`: one or more threads wait until N events complete; single use. `CyclicBarrier`: N threads wait for each other at a point; reusable. `Semaphore`: limit concurrent access to a resource with N permits (connection throttling). `Phaser` generalises barriers.

#### Q96. [basic] How do you implement producer-consumer?

Use a `BlockingQueue` (`ArrayBlockingQueue` bounded, `LinkedBlockingQueue`): producers `put` (blocks when full), consumers `take` (blocks when empty). A bounded queue provides back-pressure. Shutdown uses a poison pill or interruption. The hand-rolled `wait`/`notifyAll` version works but is easy to get wrong.

#### Q97. [intermediate] How do you stop a thread properly?

There is no safe forced stop (`Thread.stop` was removed from use and now throws `UnsupportedOperationException`). Use cooperative cancellation: `interrupt()` sets the interrupt flag, blocking methods such as `sleep` and `wait` throw `InterruptedException` and **clear** the flag. Handle it by either propagating the exception or restoring the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`. Never swallow it silently.

blocks.title: Interrupt clears the flag

blocks.code: interrupted, flag=false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### Q98. [advanced] What is ThreadLocal, and what is the leak risk?

It gives each thread its own copy of a value (per-request context, non-thread-safe helpers). In a pool, threads outlive requests, so a value set and never `remove()`d stays reachable through the thread (and can pin a classloader in app servers). Always `remove()` in `finally`. Virtual threads support `ThreadLocal` too, but with millions of threads prefer explicit parameters, or `ScopedValue` (final in Java 25, not run here).

#### Q99. [intermediate] What are virtual threads (Java 21), and when do they help?

Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier (platform) threads. When one blocks on I/O or a lock, it unmounts and the carrier runs another. They let you write simple blocking code, one thread per request, at high concurrency. They do not speed up CPU-bound work. Do not pool them; create one per task with `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or `Thread.ofVirtual().start(...)`. Before Java 24, blocking inside `synchronized` pinned the carrier; JEP 491 (Java 24) removed that for monitors.

blocks.text:
#### Q100. [advanced] Write a thread-safe lazy singleton.

The simplest correct options are an eager `static final` instance, an enum with one constant, or the holder idiom, which relies on class initialisation being thread-safe and lazy. Double-checked locking is correct only with `volatile`, because without it another thread may see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object.

blocks.title: Holder idiom and double-checked locking

blocks.text:
#### Q101. [advanced] How do atomics work? What is the ABA problem?

`AtomicInteger` and friends use compare-and-set (CAS), one hardware instruction: set the value only if it still equals what I read; otherwise retry. No lock, no blocking, but heavy contention causes many retries; `LongAdder` spreads updates across cells and sums on read, better for counters. ABA: a value changes A to B and back to A, so CAS succeeds although things changed. `AtomicStampedReference` adds a version stamp.

#### Q102. [intermediate] Concurrency versus parallelism? What makes a class thread-safe?

Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once (interleaving, possible on one core); parallelism is executing simultaneously on several cores. A class is thread-safe if it behaves correctly under any interleaving without callers adding synchronisation. The strongest strategies, in order: no shared state, immutable state, confinement to one thread, then proper locking or atomics. Document the guarantee (`@ThreadSafe` or Javadoc).

### JVM, memory and garbage collection

#### Q103. [basic] What are the JVM runtime memory areas?

Per JVM: the **heap** (all objects and arrays, split into young and old generations in generational collectors), **Metaspace** (class metadata, in native memory since Java 8, replacing PermGen), the **code cache** (JIT-compiled code), plus direct buffers and other native memory. Per thread: a **stack** (frames with locals and operand stack), a **program counter**, and a native method stack. Heap and Metaspace are shared; stacks are private.

#### Q104. [basic] What lives on the stack and what on the heap?

Local primitives and object *references* live in stack frames; every object lives on the heap, wherever the reference is. Each method call pushes a frame, popped on return. Stack memory is reclaimed automatically when the method returns, so it needs no GC. The JIT can sometimes avoid allocating a non-escaping object altogether (escape analysis, scalar replacement), but you cannot rely on it.

#### Q105. [intermediate] Explain class loading and the delegation model.

Loading finds the bytes of a class; linking verifies them, prepares static fields with default values and resolves symbols; initialisation runs static initialisers, once, when the class is first actively used. Loaders form a hierarchy: bootstrap (core `java.base`), platform, application (your classpath), and custom ones. A loader first *delegates to its parent* and only loads itself if the parent fails. This prevents user code from replacing `java.lang.String` and keeps core types unique. Two classes with the same name from different loaders are different types.

#### Q106. [intermediate] When does a class get initialised?

On first `new`, first static method call, first non-constant static field access, `Class.forName` (default), or initialisation of a subclass. Compile-time constants (`static final int X = 5`) are inlined and do not trigger it. A static initialiser that throws leaves the class unusable: `ExceptionInInitializerError` the first time, `NoClassDefFoundError` afterwards.

#### Q107. [basic] How does the garbage collector decide an object is garbage?

By *reachability*, not by reference counting. The collector starts from GC roots (live thread stacks, static fields, JNI references) and marks everything reachable; the rest is garbage. Cycles of unreachable objects are collected. Objects do not need to be set to `null` in normal code; the common exception is clearing slots in your own array-based structures (a stack that does not null popped slots leaks). **Q108. \[intermediate\] What is the generational hypothesis? How does a young collection work?** Most objects die young. The heap is divided into a young generation (eden plus two survivor spaces) and an old generation. New objects are allocated in eden. A *minor* collection copies live objects from eden and one survivor to the other survivor (cheap, since most is dead); after surviving a number of collections (the tenuring threshold, at most 15) they are promoted to old. The old generation is collected less often, by marking and compaction or concurrent cycles. Big pauses come from old-generation or full collections.

#### Q109. [intermediate] Which collectors exist, and what is the default?

Serial (single thread, tiny heaps), Parallel (throughput, multi-threaded stop-the-world), **G1** (region-based, pause-time goal, the default on server-class machines since Java 9), ZGC (concurrent, pauses in the sub-millisecond range, large heaps; generational and the default ZGC mode since Java 23) and Shenandoah (concurrent, in OpenJDK builds). The JVM picks Serial instead of G1 when it sees fewer than 2 CPUs or less than about 1.8 GB of memory; Java 27 makes G1 the default everywhere (JEP 523). Select with `-XX:+UseG1GC`, `-XX:+UseZGC`, `-XX:+UseParallelGC`.

#### Q110. [intermediate] What reference types exist?

Strong (ordinary), **soft** (cleared only when memory is needed; suited to memory-sensitive caches), **weak** (cleared at the next GC once the object is not strongly reachable; used by `WeakHashMap`), **phantom** (for post-mortem cleanup via `Cleaner`). A weak reference is cleared promptly; a soft one is kept while memory allows.

#### Q111. [intermediate] Can Java leak memory? Give examples.

Yes: not through lost pointers, but through objects that stay reachable and are never used again. Typical causes: static collections or caches that only grow; listeners or callbacks never deregistered; `ThreadLocal` values in pooled threads; mutable keys left in maps; unclosed resources (streams, connections); inner classes holding their outer instance; classloader leaks on redeploy. Diagnose with a heap dump (`jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file.hprof`) in a tool such as Eclipse MAT or VisualVM, and look at the dominator tree and GC roots.

#### Q112. [basic] Which OutOfMemoryError messages exist, and what does each mean?

`Java heap space`: the heap is full of live objects (leak or heap too small). `GC overhead limit exceeded`: the JVM spends almost all time in GC with little reclaimed. `Metaspace`: too many classes (leaks of dynamic classes, classloader leak). `unable to create native thread`: the OS refused a thread (too many threads or stack memory). `Direct buffer` `memory`: off-heap NIO buffers exhausted. `StackOverflowError` is a different error: recursion too deep for the thread's stack.

#### Q113. [intermediate] How does the JIT compiler work?

The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode and counts invocations and loop back-edges. Hot methods are compiled to machine code by tiered compilation: C1 (quick, light optimisation, with profiling) and C2 (slow to compile, aggressive optimisations based on the profile: inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling, devirtualisation). Speculation can be undone by *deoptimisation* when an assumption fails (a new subclass is loaded). This is why Java needs warm-up and why micro-benchmarks need JMH. Code is stored in the code cache (default 240 MB on this build).

#### Q114. [basic] Which JVM flags matter most for memory?

`-Xms` and `-Xmx` (initial and maximum heap; setting them equal avoids resizing pauses), `-Xss` (thread stack size, default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux), `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`, `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` (container-friendly sizing), `-XX:+UseG1GC`/`-XX:+UseZGC`, `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` (G1 target, default 200), `-Xlog:gc*`, `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`. On the build machine (8 GB RAM) the default maximum heap was about 1.5 GB, one quarter of physical memory; `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` shows every effective value.

blocks.title: Default sizing on the build machine (JDK 21, 8 GB RAM, 2 CPUs)

blocks.text:
#### Q115. [intermediate] A production service is slow or hung. What do you do?

Gather evidence before changing anything. `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` or `jstack` shows what threads are doing (deadlocks, a pool exhausted, everything waiting on I/O). `jstat -gc <pid> 1000` and GC logs show GC pressure. `jcmd` `<pid> GC.heap_info` and a heap dump show memory. Java Flight Recorder (`-XX:StartFlightRecording` or `jcmd <pid>` `JFR.start`) records CPU, allocation, locks and I/O with low overhead. Take several thread dumps a few seconds apart; one dump is a photograph, several show movement.

#### Q116. [intermediate] What are compact strings and string deduplication?

Since Java 9, `String` stores its characters in a `byte[]` plus a coder flag: Latin-1 text uses one byte per character, other text two (UTF-16). Roughly halves memory for typical text. G1 can additionally deduplicate identical backing arrays of strings (`-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`, off by default). `intern()` shares strings through the pool, but a pool grown unboundedly is a leak risk.

#### Q117. [advanced] How big is an object?

An object has a header (mark word and class pointer; about 12 bytes with compressed class pointers on 64-bit HotSpot), then fields, padded to a multiple of 8 bytes. So `new Object()` is 16 bytes and an `Integer` is 16. Compressed oops (references as 32-bit offsets) are on by default for heaps under about 32 GB. Compact object headers (`-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`, product feature in Java 25, on by default in Java 27 per JEP 534) shrink the header to 8 bytes. Use the JOL library to inspect layouts. Arrays add a 4-byte length.

#### Q118. [basic] What is Metaspace, and how does it differ from PermGen?

PermGen was a fixed-size region of the heap holding class metadata and interned strings (before Java 7), prone to `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`. Java 8 replaced it with Metaspace in native memory, which grows on demand and is limited only by `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` (unlimited by default) or the OS. Interned strings moved to the heap in Java 7. Static fields' values live in the heap, with the class's mirror object.

**Q119. \[intermediate\] "Java Memory Model" versus "JVM memory structure": are they the same?** No, and interviewers like to check. The runtime memory structure (heap, stacks, Metaspace) describes where data lives. The Java Memory Model (JLS chapter 17) defines the rules for visibility and ordering of reads and writes between threads. Mixing them up is a common red flag.

#### Q120. [intermediate] Should you call System.gc() or use finalizers?

No. `System.gc()` is only a hint (it triggered a full pause in the log above: `Pause Full (System.gc())`) and can hurt latency; `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` ignores it. Finalizers are deprecated for removal: unpredictable timing, resurrection and performance cost. For cleanup use try-with-resources and `AutoCloseable`; for a safety net use `java.lang.ref.Cleaner`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Walk me through what happens when you run `new Order()` in terms of memory." The class is loaded and initialised if this is the first use (Metaspace holds its metadata). The JVM allocates space for the object in eden, normally by bumping a thread-local allocation buffer pointer (TLAB), which is why allocation is fast. Header and fields are zeroed, then the constructor chain runs. The reference is stored in a stack slot or a field. When no GC root can reach the object it becomes garbage and is reclaimed in a young collection, or promoted to old if it survives enough collections.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Containerised Spring Boot services should set heap relative to the container (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`), enable GC logging and heap-dump-on-OOM, expose thread and heap metrics through Micrometer, and keep a JFR recording available. A pod killed by the container runtime without a Java OOM usually means total native memory (Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers) exceeded the limit, not the heap alone.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Concurrency and JVM answers must come from models, not memorised slogans.

- Shared mutable state needs happens-before: locks, volatile, atomics, safe publication; volatile is not atomic.
- Prefer executors, bounded queues and concurrent collections to raw threads; handle interrupts and exceptions deliberately.
- Virtual threads make blocking cheap; they do not make CPU work faster.
- Reachability, not reference counts, defines garbage; leaks are reachable-but-unused objects.
- Know the areas (heap, Metaspace, stacks), G1/ZGC basics, and the commands: `jcmd`, `jstack`, `jstat`, heap dump, JFR.

Interviewers use this group to find out whether you have kept up with the language and whether you can design code that other people can live with. For the modern-Java questions, always say *which release* finalised a feature; that single habit separates people who read the release notes from people who memorised a list. Questions continue the numbering of the previous chapters and are not repeated from them.

### Language and library features, Java 8 to 25

#### Q121. [basic] Which Java versions are LTS, and which one should a new project use?

Long-term-support releases are 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 (September 2025); since Java 17 a new LTS arrives every two years, and a non-LTS feature release appears every March and September. A new project should target the newest LTS that its frameworks support, today Java 25 (or 21 if a dependency lags). Non-LTS releases are supported for six months only, so they suit experiments and early feedback, not long-lived production services. Java 26 (March 2026) and 27 (September 2026) are such releases.

#### Q122. [basic] What are records, and what do you get for free?

A record is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier (final in Java 16). From the component list the compiler generates a private final field per component, a canonical constructor, accessors named like the components (`r.lo()`, not `getLo()`), and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` based on all components. A record cannot extend a class and cannot declare instance fields beyond its components, but it can implement interfaces, have static members and extra constructors.

blocks.title: Compact constructor validates; equals is by value

blocks.text:
#### Q123. [intermediate] Are records really immutable?

Only shallowly. The fields are final, but a component that refers to a mutable object can still be changed through that object. A record holding a `List` shows later additions to the caller's list. A record holding an array also compares arrays by reference in the generated `equals`. Defend in the compact constructor: `this.items = List.copyOf(items)` (a compact constructor assigns the parameters, so write `items = List.copyOf(items);`).

blocks.title: Shallow immutability and array components (run on JDK 21)

blocks.text:
#### Q124. [basic] What is a sealed type, and why does it matter?

`sealed` (final in Java 17) restricts which classes may extend or implement a type, listed in `permits` (or inferred when all are in the same file). Each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`. The payoff is that the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, so a `switch` over the type can be checked for exhaustiveness without a `default`, and adding a new subtype turns every incomplete switch into a compile error. Sealed types plus records give you algebraic data types, the Java way to model "one of these shapes".

#### Q125. [intermediate] Explain pattern matching for switch and record patterns.

Pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16) tests and binds in one step: `if (o instanceof String s && s.length() >` `3)`. Pattern matching for `switch` (final in Java 21) lets `case` labels be type patterns with optional `when` guards, and `case` `null` is allowed. Record patterns (also Java 21) deconstruct a record in the label and may nest: `case Rect(double w,` `double h) -> w * h`. A switch expression must be exhaustive; for a sealed hierarchy the compiler checks it. Order matters: a more general label before a more specific one is a compile error (dominance).

blocks.text:
No `default` is needed: remove the `Tri` cases and the code no longer compiles.

#### Q126. [intermediate] What does case null change in a switch?

Before Java 21 a `switch` on a reference threw `NullPointerException` for `null`. With pattern switches you may write `case null -> ...` (alone or as `case null, default`). Without it, `null` still throws, so old code keeps its behaviour. This makes "handle everything including null" a single expression.

blocks.title: Switch on Object with null and a guard (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q127. [basic] Switch expression versus switch statement?

A switch *expression* (Java 14) produces a value, uses `->` arms that do not fall through, and must be exhaustive; use `yield` to return a value from a block arm. The classic *statement* with `case X:` falls through unless you `break`, which is the source of many bugs. Prefer arrows even in statements.

blocks.title: yield inside a block arm

blocks.text:
#### Q128. [basic] What are text blocks?

Multi-line string literals delimited by `"""` (Java 15). The compiler removes the common leading indentation (determined by the closing delimiter and the least-indented line), normalises line endings to `\n`, and allows quotes without escaping. A trailing backslash joins lines, and `\s` keeps a trailing space. They are ideal for JSON, SQL and HTML in code and tests.

blocks.title: A text block with a joined line

blocks.text:
#### Q129. [basic] What does var do? When should you avoid it?

`var` (Java 10) infers a *local variable's* static type from its initialiser; it is not dynamic typing and the type is still fixed at compile time. It works for locals, `for` variables and lambda parameters, but not for fields, parameters, return types or `var x = null`. Use it when the type is obvious from the right-hand side (`var users = new ArrayList<User>()`), avoid it when it hides information (`var x = service.process()`), and keep the diamond meaningful: `var list = new` `ArrayList<>()` infers `ArrayList<Object>`.

#### Q130. [intermediate] What are sequenced collections (Java 21)?

Three new interfaces, `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet` and `SequencedMap`, give every collection with a defined encounter order the same methods: `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast`, `removeFirst`, `removeLast` and `reversed()` (a live view). `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet`, `LinkedHashMap` and `SortedSet`/`SortedMap` types implement them. Before this, getting the last element of a `List` was `list.get(list.size() - 1)` and of a `LinkedHashSet` required iteration.

blocks.title: Sequenced collections (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text: **Q131. \[intermediate\] Difference between List.of, Collections.unmodifiableList and Stream.toList()?** `List.of(...)` creates a truly immutable list: `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and `null` elements are rejected with `NullPointerException`. `Collections.unmodifiableList(src)` is only an unmodifiable *view*: you cannot change it through the view, but changes to `src` show through. `List.copyOf(src)` is a snapshot. `Stream.toList()` (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list but, unlike `List.of`, allows `null` elements; `Collectors.toList()` gives an unspecified, in practice modifiable, `ArrayList`.

blocks.title: View versus copy (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q132. [intermediate] What are virtual threads, and what do they not fix?

Finalised in Java 21 (JEP 444). A virtual thread is a `Thread` scheduled by the JVM instead of the OS: it is mounted on a small pool of carrier (platform) threads and unmounted when it blocks on I/O, so you can run hundreds of thousands of them. Use them for blocking, request-per-thread code: `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)`. They do not speed up CPU-bound work, should not be pooled (create one per task), and until Java 24 a virtual thread blocked inside `synchronized` pinned its carrier (JEP 491 removed that pinning in 24). Limit concurrency to scarce resources (a database) with a `Semaphore`, not with a pool size. **Q133. \[advanced\] What are scoped values and structured concurrency, and what is their status?** `ScopedValue` (final in Java 25, JEP 506) shares immutable data with a method call tree and its child threads in a bounded scope; it is a cheaper, safer replacement for most `ThreadLocal` use with virtual threads. Structured concurrency (`StructuredTaskScope`) treats a group of subtasks as one unit of work whose lifetime is bounded by a block, so failure and cancellation propagate; it is still a *preview* API in Java 25, and in the later releases (JEPs 525, 533), so it needs `--enable-preview` and its shape may still change. State the status exactly; do not call it final.

#### Q134. [intermediate] What do Optional and its misuse look like?

`Optional<T>` is a return type that says "there may be no result" and makes callers handle it with `map`, `flatMap`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow`, `ifPresentOrElse` and `or`. Misuse: as a field, as a method parameter, in collections, calling `get()` without checking (use `orElseThrow()`), or `Optional.of(x)` with a possible null (use `ofNullable`). `orElse(expr)` always evaluates `expr`; use `orElseGet(supplier)` when it is expensive.

blocks.code:
Optional<String> op = Optional.of("x");
System.out.println(op.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("none"));                 // X
System.out.println(Optional.ofNullable((String) null)
        .or(() -> Optional.of("fallback")).get());                              // fallback
