blocks.text:
#### Q135. [intermediate] What useful String and Stream methods arrived after Java 8?

`String`: `isBlank`, `strip`, `lines`, `repeat` (11), `formatted`, `stripIndent` (15), `indent`, `transform`. `Stream`: `takeWhile`, `dropWhile`, the three-argument `iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` (9), `Stream.toList()` (16), `mapMulti` (16) and `Gatherers` with `gather` (final in Java 24, JEP 485) for custom intermediate operations such as windowing. `Optional`: `ifPresentOrElse`, `or`, `stream`, `isEmpty`.

blocks.code:
System.out.println(Stream.iterate(1, i -> i < 50, i -> i * 3).toList());  // [1, 3, 9, 27]
System.out.println("a,b,,".split(",").length);        // 2 (trailing empties dropped)
System.out.println("  hi ".strip() + "|" + " ".isBlank() + "ab".repeat(2));  // hi|trueabab
blocks.title: Bounded iterate and the split pitfall (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q136. [intermediate] How do you make an HTTP call without a library?

`java.net.http.HttpClient` (Java 11): build one client, reuse it, create an `HttpRequest`, and call `send` (blocking) or `sendAsync` (returns a `CompletableFuture`). It supports HTTP/2 by default and WebSocket; Java 26 adds HTTP/3 support (JEP 517). In services you normally use the framework's client (Spring `RestClient`/`WebClient`), but the JDK client is fine for small tools and tests.

blocks.title: Skeleton of a GET (not run: needs network)

blocks.text:
#### Q137. [intermediate] What changed for running small programs?

Since Java 11 `java Hello.java` compiles and runs one source file without a separate `javac` step. Java 25 finalises compact source files and instance `main` methods (JEP 512): a file can contain a top-level `void main()` with no class, no `static` and no `String[] args`, plus the `IO.println` helper. Java 25 also finalises module import declarations (`import` `module java.base;`, JEP 511) and flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513), which allow statements before `super(...)` as long as they do not use `this`. These are for teaching, scripting and validation code; they do not change how real applications are structured.

#### Q138. [advanced] What are unnamed variables and patterns?

Final in Java 22 (JEP 456): the underscore `_` declares a variable or pattern you intend not to use, for example `catch` `(NumberFormatException _)`, `for (var _ : list)` or `case Rect(double w, _)`. It documents intent and the compiler will not warn about it. It is not allowed to refer to it later. This is a syntax feature, not a runtime one. **Q139. \[advanced\] What is new at the JVM level in Java 24 and 25 that a backend engineer should**

#### know?

Items that are confirmed: compact object headers (JEP 519, product feature in Java 25, enabled with `-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`, shrinking the header from 12 to 8 bytes in typical configurations and reducing heap use; JEP 534 makes it the default in Java 27); virtual threads no longer pin on `synchronized` (24); AOT class loading and linking and AOT method profiling to speed start-up (24, 25); generational ZGC as the only ZGC mode (non-generational was removed in 24); the Security Manager removed for good (24). Say that you would measure on your own workload before adopting any of them.

#### Q140. [intermediate] Explain the Stream Collectors you use most.

`toList`, `toSet`, `toMap(key, value, merge)` (the two-argument form throws `IllegalStateException` on duplicate keys), `groupingBy(classifier, downstream)` for a `Map<K, List<V>>` or counts and sums, `partitioningBy(predicate)` for a two-key map, `joining`, `counting`, `summingInt`, `averagingDouble`, `mapping`, `teeing` (two collectors combined, Java 12). `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList` exists when you need immutability.

blocks.title: partitioningBy always has both keys (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q141. [intermediate] What was removed or deprecated that candidates still mention?

`finalize()` is deprecated for removal (Java 18); use try-with-resources or `Cleaner`. The Security Manager was removed in Java 24. The Applet API was removed in Java 26. `Thread.stop`, `suspend` and `resume` are dead; the `Date`/`Calendar` classes remain but are replaced in new code by `java.time`. PermGen vanished in Java 8, Nashorn in 15, and CMS in 14. Knowing what is gone prevents recommending it in a design review.

#### Q142. [advanced] How would you adopt a new LTS in a large codebase?

Treat it as a controlled migration. Build and test on the new JDK in CI next to the old one; fix removed APIs and illegal reflective access (`--add-opens` flags as a short-term bridge); upgrade the build plugins, bytecode libraries (ASM, Byte Buddy) and frameworks first; read the release's compatibility notes; run the same load test and compare GC logs and latency; roll out gradually (canary) and keep an easy rollback. Adopt new language features only after the runtime change is stable, in separate commits.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Modern Java questions reward precision about which release made what final.

- Records, sealed types and pattern matching together model data safely; the compiler enforces exhaustiveness.
- Records are only shallowly immutable; copy mutable components in the compact constructor.
- Virtual threads make blocking cheap but do not speed up CPU work; scoped values are final in 25, structured concurrency is still preview.
- Know the immutable-collection family (`List.of`, `copyOf`, `unmodifiableList`, `toList`) and what each allows.
- Plan LTS upgrades as a tested migration, not a version bump.

sections.title: Interview Q&A: Design and Best Practices

blocks.text:
The last group of questions has no single correct answer, so interviewers listen for reasoning: what you optimise for, what it costs, and how you would test it. Give a rule, a reason, and an exception. Use the small domain below (orders and notifications) for your own examples when you answer aloud.

### Object-oriented design and SOLID

#### Q143. [basic] State the SOLID principles in one sentence each.

**S**ingle responsibility: a class has one reason to change. **O**pen/closed: extend behaviour by adding code (new implementations), not by editing tested code. **L**iskov substitution: a subtype must be usable wherever its supertype is expected without surprising the caller (same contracts, no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions). **I**nterface segregation: many small, client-specific interfaces beat one fat interface. **D**ependency inversion: high-level policy depends on abstractions, and details (databases, email) implement them. These are heuristics for managing change, not laws.

#### Q144. [intermediate] Give a Liskov violation in Java.

The classic one: `Square extends Rectangle` and overrides `setWidth` to also change the height; code that sets width and height independently and then asserts the area breaks. A real example from the JDK: `List.of(...)` is a `List` that throws `UnsupportedOperationException` from `add`, which is why the `List` contract allows optional operations and why you should document or encode mutability in types. Fix by modelling the true relationship (a shared `Shape` interface), or prefer composition.

#### Q145. [intermediate] What is dependency injection, and do you need a framework?

Dependency injection means an object receives its collaborators from outside (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them with `new`. That makes the class depend on an interface and lets tests pass a fake. You do not need a framework to do it; Spring, Guice or Jakarta CDI just automate wiring, scoping and lifecycle. Prefer constructor injection: dependencies are `final`, mandatory and visible, and the object is never half-built.

blocks.title: Constructor injection with a test double (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
**Q146. \[intermediate\] Composition or inheritance, and what is the fragile base class problem?** Prefer composition. A subclass depends on how its parent calls its own overridable methods, so a harmless-looking change in the parent can break children (for example `HashSet.addAll` calling `add`, which a counting subclass also overrides, double counts). If you design a class for inheritance, document the self-use of overridable methods; otherwise make it `final` or give it a non-public constructor. Inheritance is right for a true is-a relationship with a stable, designed-for-extension parent.

#### Q147. [intermediate] How do you make a class immutable?

Declare the class `final` (or use a record), make all fields `private final`, set them only in the constructor, provide no setters, make defensive copies of mutable inputs *and* outputs (`List.copyOf`, `clone` of arrays, `Date` avoided), and do not leak `this` from the constructor. Benefits: thread safety without locks, safe as map keys, simple reasoning, safe caching. Cost: allocate a new object per change, which is usually cheap.

blocks.title: An immutable value class (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
Money never stores amounts as `double`; `long` cents or `BigDecimal` avoids rounding errors.

#### Q148. [intermediate] When do you use the Builder pattern?

When a type has many optional parameters or must be validated as a whole before construction. A builder gives named, readable calls, lets the target be immutable, and builds only when `build()` is called. The telescoping-constructor alternative is unreadable at five arguments. For a record with few components the canonical constructor is enough, and a static factory method with a good name (`Money.of`, `List.of`) often beats a builder.

blocks.title: Builder producing an immutable object (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q149. [intermediate] How do you implement a singleton, and should you?

The safest simple way is a single-element `enum` (serialization and reflection safe), or a holder class for lazy initialisation. Most "singletons" in real applications are managed by the container (a Spring bean with singleton scope) and injected, which keeps them testable. Hand-written global singletons hide dependencies and make tests share state; use them only for genuinely process-wide, stateless or thread-safe things.

blocks.title: Enum singleton (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q150. [intermediate] Strategy and Factory in modern Java: do you still need classes?

Often a lambda or a method reference replaces a one-method strategy class. A map from a name to a function is a tiny factory/registry. Keep real classes when the strategy has state, several methods, or needs a name in logs and tests.

blocks.code:
Map<String, BinaryOperator<Integer>> ops = Map.of("add", Integer::sum, "mul", (x, y) -> x * y);
System.out.println(ops.get("mul").apply(6, 7));    // 42
blocks.title: Strategy as a map of functions (JDK 21 output)

blocks.text:
#### Q151. [intermediate] What other patterns do you meet daily in Java code?

Observer (listeners, event buses), Decorator (`BufferedInputStream` wraps an `InputStream`), Template method (`AbstractList`, Spring's `JdbcTemplate`), Iterator (`Iterable`), Adapter (`Arrays.asList`), Proxy (dynamic proxies behind Spring AOP and `@Transactional`), Builder, Factory method (`List.of`, `Optional.of`), and Singleton as a scope. Name the pattern, the problem it solves and a JDK example; interviewers care more about the example than the name.

**Q152. \[advanced\] What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface now that**

#### interfaces have default methods?

An interface still has no instance state and no constructors, and a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. Abstract classes hold shared state and enforce construction, and can have non-public members. Use an interface for a capability or a contract (often with a few `default` helpers, evolving an API without breaking implementers); use an abstract class when subclasses share fields and a skeleton algorithm. A common pairing: interface plus a skeletal abstract class (as `List` and `AbstractList`).

### Writing code others can maintain

#### Q153. [basic] What makes a good method or class name and size?

A name states the intent in the domain's words (`calculateShippingCost`, not `process`), a method does one thing at one level of abstraction, and a class has a clear responsibility that you can state in one sentence. Long parameter lists (more than about four) usually signal a missing type. Size is a symptom, not a rule: split when you find yourself writing comments to separate sections.

#### Q154. [intermediate] How should you handle null?

Do not return `null` for collections (return empty ones); use `Optional` for "no result" in return values; validate arguments at public boundaries with `Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x")` so failure is early and clear; use `Objects.equals` when either side can be null; annotate intent (`@Nullable`) where tooling supports it. Make fields non-null by construction. The "billion-dollar mistake" is not that null exists but that types do not say where it is allowed.

#### Q155. [intermediate] When do you use checked versus unchecked exceptions in your own API?

Use a checked exception when the caller can reasonably recover and the failure is part of the contract (a file may be missing); use an unchecked one for programming errors (`IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`) and for failures the caller cannot handle meaningfully. Many modern libraries, including Spring, prefer unchecked exceptions to avoid `throws` clauses leaking through layers. Whatever you choose, include context in the message, wrap the cause, and translate low-level exceptions at layer boundaries (`SQLException` should not reach the controller).

#### Q156. [intermediate] How do you log properly?

Log through a facade (SLF4J) with levels: `ERROR` for failures needing attention, `WARN` for suspicious but handled cases, `INFO` for business milestones, `DEBUG` and `TRACE` for diagnosis. Use parameterised messages (`log.info("order {}` `placed", id)`) rather than string concatenation, log an exception once with its stack trace and cause (`log.error("payment failed for {}", id, e)`), never log secrets or personal data, and include a correlation or trace ID so one request can be followed across services. Do not both log and rethrow at every layer, or one failure appears ten times.

#### Q157. [intermediate] What makes a good unit test?

It is fast, isolated, deterministic and checks one behaviour, with a name that states it (`rejectsNegativeAmounts`). Arrange, act, assert. Inject the clock, random source and I/O so that results are repeatable. Prefer real small objects over mocks, and mock only the boundary (HTTP clients, repositories). Keep a pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests (database through Testcontainers), few end-to-end tests. Coverage numbers show what is not tested, not that the tested parts are right.

#### Q158. [intermediate] How do you handle equals/hashCode, toString and Comparable in domain

#### classes?

Records give you value `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` for free. For classes, implement `equals` and `hashCode` from the same business fields, and never from fields that change while the object sits in a hash set. For JPA entities base equality on the identifier or a natural key, with a constant `hashCode` or a careful implementation, because generated IDs are `null` before saving. Keep `compareTo` consistent with `equals`, or document why not (`BigDecimal` is the famous exception). Never put secrets in `toString`.

#### Q159. [advanced] What do you watch for in API design?

Make misuse hard: immutable inputs, no flag parameters (two methods instead of `process(true)`), strong types over `String` and `int` (a `CustomerId` record), return the narrowest useful type, accept the broadest (`Collection` or `Iterable`, or a functional interface), keep the surface small because everything public is a promise, document the contract (null handling, thread-safety, exceptions), and deprecate before removing. Prefer returning empty collections to `null`, and avoid exposing internal mutable state.

#### Q160. [advanced] How do you approach performance work?

Measure first. Define the target (p99 latency, throughput), reproduce with a realistic load, find the bottleneck with a profiler or JFR (CPU, allocation, locks, I/O), change one thing, and measure again. Typical wins are algorithms and data structures (a `HashMap` instead of a list scan), fewer allocations in hot loops, batching I/O and database round trips, caching with an eviction policy, and fixing N+1 queries, long before micro-tuning. Micro-benchmarks need JMH because the JIT, warm-up and dead-code elimination distort naive timing loops.

#### Q161. [advanced] How do you design a thread-safe, in-memory cache in an interview?

State the requirements first: size bound, eviction (LRU or TTL), concurrency level, loading behaviour. A start: `ConcurrentHashMap<K, V>` with `computeIfAbsent` so concurrent misses for one key load only once (keep the loader short and never touch the same map from inside it), plus a bound and eviction. For LRU, `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` and `removeEldestEntry` guarded by a lock is simplest. In production say you would use Caffeine (size and time-based eviction, statistics, async loading) rather than write your own, and discuss stale data and stampedes.

#### Q162. [advanced] A service gets slow in production. What is your first hour?

Establish facts before changing anything. Check recent deploys and config; look at the dashboard (latency, error rate, saturation: CPU, memory, GC pauses, thread-pool queues, connection-pool waits); read GC logs and take two or three thread dumps with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` to see where threads wait; check downstream dependencies and the database slow-query log; capture a short JFR recording. Roll back or shed load if users are hurting, then find the cause. Afterwards write the timeline and a regression test or alert so it cannot return silently.

#### Q163. [intermediate] How do you review code, and what do you look for?

Correctness and edge cases first (null, empty, overflow, concurrency, resource closing), then design (fits the structure, no duplicated logic, right abstraction), tests (do they fail without the change?), naming and readability, security (input validation, injection, secrets), and operability (logs, metrics, config). Comment on the code, not the person; explain *why*; separate must-fix from preference; approve quickly when the risk is low. Small pull requests are the best review tool.

#### Q164. [intermediate] How do you keep dependencies and builds healthy?

Pin versions through a BOM or dependency management, update regularly in small steps (automated update pull requests), scan for known vulnerabilities in CI, prefer few well-maintained libraries over many, avoid depending on a library's internals, and keep builds reproducible (`mvn -B verify` or `gradle build` from a clean checkout must pass). Separate API modules from implementations so that you can change one without recompiling everything.

#### Q165. [basic] Why should we hire you? Tell us about a project in Java.

Prepare a two-minute story with this shape: the problem and the users, your role, one design decision with its alternatives and why you chose what you did, one thing that went wrong and what you learned, and a measurable result (latency reduced, tests added, bug rate lowered). Choose a project you can discuss several layers deep, because the interviewer will follow your answer down to the code. Honest scope beats inflated claims: "I built this part, I read that part" is credible.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Design answers are arguments: a rule, the reason, the cost, the exception.

- Prefer constructor injection, composition and immutability; they make code testable and thread-safe.
- Patterns are named solutions; know a JDK example for each and whether a lambda is enough.
- Validate at boundaries, return empty collections, wrap and contextualise exceptions, log once with the cause.
- Measure before optimising; diagnose production with dashboards, thread dumps, GC logs and JFR.
- Prepare one project story you can defend several layers deep.

sections.title: What Does This Print? Fifty Puzzles

blocks.text:
Interviewers love small programs whose output surprises you, and not because they are cruel. A snippet that tests boxing, initialisation order or overload resolution shows in thirty seconds whether you have a mental model of the language or only a habit of typing code until it works. This chapter gives you fifty such snippets. Every output below was produced by running the listing on OpenJDK 21; where a result depends on the machine it says so.

#### How to use the puzzles

Cover the output and the explanation. Read the code once, write your prediction on paper, and only then look. A wrong prediction is the valuable case: it points at a rule you had wrong. After the explanation, ask "which rule decided this?" and name it (for example "constant folding", "most specific overload", "left operand evaluated first"). Naming the rule is what you will do in an interview.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How should I answer a "what does this print" question? Do not blurt out an answer. Walk through the evaluation order aloud, name the rule that applies at each step, and then state the output. If you are unsure between two outcomes, say which rule would decide it. Interviewers reward visible reasoning, and a wrong answer with a correct method often scores higher than a lucky right one.

Each puzzle is labelled basic, intermediate or advanced. Treat any puzzle you got wrong as a flashcard to revisit in a few days. The listings are complete programs; save one as `P01.java` and run it with `java P01.java`.

### Boxing, identity and the string pool

#### Puzzle 1. Integer cache and equals across wrapper types (basic)

blocks.title: P01.java

blocks.code:
$ java P01.java
true
false
true
false
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`Integer.valueOf` (which autoboxing calls) returns cached objects for -128..127, so `a == b` compares the same object. 128 is outside the cache, so `c` and `d` are two different objects and `==` compares references. `equals` compares values and is the right tool. The last two lines mix wrapper types: `Long.equals(Object)` first checks that the argument is a `Long`, and the autoboxed `128` is an `Integer`, so it is `false`. In `big == 128` one operand is a primitive, so `big` is unboxed and the comparison is numeric.

#### Puzzle 2. More wrapper identity (intermediate)

blocks.title: P02.java

blocks.code:
$ java P02.java
false
true
true
true
true
true
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Only `Integer` (and `Long`, `Short`, `Byte`, `Character` up to 127) have caches; `Boolean` has two instances; `Double` and `Float` have no cache, so two boxed `1.0` values are different objects. `i1 == i3` is `true` because one side is a primitive `int`, which forces unboxing. Never rely on identity of wrappers: use `equals` or unbox first.

#### Puzzle 3. Literal, new String and intern (basic)

blocks.title: P03.java

blocks.code:
$ java P03.java
true
false
true
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Literals with equal text share one pooled object, so `s1 == s2`. `new String("java")` always creates a fresh heap object, so `s1 == s3` is `false`, though `equals` is `true`. `intern()` returns the pooled instance, which is the same object as the literal. In real code compare strings with `equals`; the pool is an optimisation, not a contract.

#### Puzzle 4. Compile-time constants and concatenation (intermediate)

blocks.title: P04.java

blocks.code:
$ java P04.java
true
false
true
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`"hel" + "lo"` is a constant expression, so the compiler folds it to `"hello"` and it is pooled: `a == b`. `hel + "lo"` uses a non-final variable, so the concatenation happens at run time and creates a new object. Declaring the variable `final` makes it a constant variable, which is folded again, so `a == d` is `true`. Interning the run-time result gives the pooled instance.

#### Puzzle 5. Strings are immutable, StringBuilder has no equals (basic)

blocks.title: P05.java

blocks.code:
$ java P05.java
false
true
0
abc
ABCDEF
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`StringBuilder` does not override `equals`, so it uses identity. `compareTo` (since Java 11) compares contents, giving `0`. `String` methods never change the receiver: `concat` and `toUpperCase` return new strings, and ignoring the result does nothing. Reassign the result if you want it.

### Initialization order and dispatch

#### Puzzle 6. Static and instance initialisation (basic)

blocks.title: P06.java

blocks.code:
$ java P06.java
init x
static block
main starts
init y
instance block
constructor
init y
instance block
constructor
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Static initialisers run once, when the class is first initialised (here before `main`'s first line, because `main` is in the same class), in textual order. Each `new` then runs field initialisers and instance blocks in textual order, followed by the constructor body. Mixing the order of the field and the block would change the output, so keep initialisers at the top of the class.

#### Puzzle 7. Overridable method called from a constructor (intermediate)

blocks.title: P07.java

blocks.code:
$ java P07.java
Child.show null 0
Child ctor child
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The `Base` constructor runs before `Child`'s field initialisers, but dynamic dispatch already selects `Child.show`. The fields still hold their default values (`null` and `0`) because `Child`'s initialisers have not run. Calling an overridable method from a constructor exposes a half-built object: make the method `private` or `final`, or do the work in a factory method.

#### Puzzle 8. Class and constructor chain order (intermediate)

blocks.title: P08.java

blocks.code:
$ java P08.java
Parent static
Child static
Parent instance
Parent ctor
Child instance
Child ctor(int)
Child ctor()
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The sequence is: superclass static, subclass static (once per class load), then for each instance the superclass initialisers and constructor, then the subclass initialisers and the constructor chain. `Child()` calls `this(1)`, which calls `super()`, so the instance block of `Child` runs once, inside the constructor that calls `super()`, never twice.

#### Puzzle 9. When is a class initialised? (advanced)

blocks.title: P09.java

blocks.code:
$ java P09.java
100
between
Config initialised
200
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`LIMIT` is a compile-time constant (`static final` primitive with a constant initialiser). The compiler copies the value into `main`, so reading it never touches `Config` and its static block does not run. `BOXED` is not a constant (`Integer` is an object), so the first access initialises the class. This is why changing a constant in a library needs recompiling its users.

#### Puzzle 10. Fields and static methods are not virtual (intermediate)

blocks.title: P10.java

blocks.code:
$ java P10.java
animal
dog
Dog.who
Animal.kind
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Only instance methods are dispatched on the run-time type. Fields and static methods are resolved with the declared type: `a` is an `Animal`, so `a.name` and `a.kind()` use `Animal`'s versions, while `a.who()` runs `Dog.who`. Cast to `Dog` to see the hiding field. Avoid hiding fields; call static methods through the class name.

#### Puzzle 11. Private methods are not overridden (intermediate)

blocks.title: P11.java

blocks.code:
$ java P11.java
A.hello
B.hello
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`A.call()` calls `hello()`; because `A.hello` is private it is bound at compile time to `A`'s version and `B.hello` is an unrelated method that merely has the same name. Without `private`, the call would dispatch to `B.hello`. Adding `@Override` to `B.hello` would be a compile error, which is exactly why you should use the annotation.

#### Puzzle 12. Default method resolution (advanced)

blocks.title: P12.java

blocks.code:
$ java P12.java
Base
B
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The rules in order: a class method (even inherited) wins over any interface default, so `C` prints `Base`. Otherwise the most specific interface wins: `B` extends `A`, so for `D` the default from `B` is chosen even though `A` is listed too. Only two unrelated interfaces with the same default cause a compile error that you must resolve with `A.super.hi()`.

### Overloads, varargs and the ternary operator

#### Puzzle 13. Overload resolution phases (intermediate)

blocks.title: P13.java

blocks.code:
$ java P13.java
String
Integer
Object
long
long
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The compiler tries three phases in order: no boxing and no varargs; then boxing; then varargs. `m(42)` needs boxing, and `Integer` is more specific than `Object`. `n(5)` finds `n(long)` in phase 1 by widening, so it wins over boxing to `Integer`, and varargs is never considered. `m((Object) "text")` picks `m(Object)` because overloads are chosen from the static type.

#### Puzzle 14. Most specific method (advanced)

blocks.title: P14.java

blocks.code:
$ java P14.java
char[]
float
float
double
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`p(null)`: both `Object` and `char[]` accept `null`; `char[]` is a subtype of `Object` and therefore more specific. (With `String` and `Integer` overloads it would be an ambiguity error.) For `q(1)` and `q(1L)`, both `float` and `double` are reachable by widening, and `float` is more specific because it widens to `double`. Only the literal `1.0` is a `double`.

#### Puzzle 15. Varargs and null (advanced)

blocks.title: P15.java

blocks.code:
$ java P15.java
len 0
len 1
null array
len 2
len 1
1 3
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`f()` creates an empty array. `f((String) null)` passes one element that is `null`, giving an array of length 1. `f((String[]) null)` passes the array itself as `null`. The cast on `g` decides whether the array is the argument list or a single element. `Arrays.asList(int[])` cannot spread a primitive array, so you get a list with one element of type `int[]`; with `Integer[]` you get three elements.

#### Puzzle 16. Ternary typing rules (advanced)

blocks.title: P16.java

blocks.code:
$ java P16.java
1 1.0
a
97
NPE from unboxing
null
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
If one branch is a numeric type and the other is a different numeric type, the result is promoted: `flag ? 1 : 2.0` is `1.0`. A `char` and an `int` constant that fits in a `char` stay a `char` (prints `a`); a non-constant `int` variable promotes to `int` (prints `97`). If one branch is a primitive and the other is an `Integer`, the result is the primitive, so a `null Integer` is unboxed and throws a `NullPointerException`. With `null` and `int` literal, the result type is `Integer`, so no unboxing occurs.

#### Puzzle 17. Static call on null, instanceof, println(char[]) (intermediate)

blocks.title: P17.java

blocks.code:
$ java P17.java
hello
false
false
hi
true
hi
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
A static method is resolved from the declared type, so `u.hello()` does not dereference `u` and works even if `u` is `null`. `instanceof` is `false` for `null`, so it never throws. `println(char[])` is a special overload that prints the characters, but string concatenation calls `String.valueOf(Object)`, which gives the type-and-hash form such as `[C@1b6d3586`. That is why the code checks only the prefix.

### Control flow, finally and exceptions

#### Puzzle 18. Return and finally (intermediate)

blocks.title: P18.java

blocks.code:
$ java P18.java
2
10
ab
3
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The return value is computed first, then `finally` runs. For the primitive in `b()` the saved copy is `10`, so changing `x` later has no effect. In `c()` the saved value is a reference, so the mutation inside `finally` is visible: `ab`. A `return` inside `finally` replaces the result of the `try` and even discards a thrown exception, as in `d()`. Never return from `finally`; the compiler warns about it.

#### Puzzle 19. try-with-resources, close order and suppression (advanced)

blocks.title: P19.java

blocks.code:
$ java P19.java
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
caught body failed
suppressed close B
suppressed close A
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Resources close in reverse order of opening, before the `catch` block runs. The body's exception is the primary one; the exceptions thrown by both `close` calls are attached as suppressed exceptions and read with `getSuppressed()`. In a hand-written `try/finally`, an exception from `close` would hide the real failure.

#### Puzzle 20. Short-circuit and non-short-circuit operators (intermediate)

blocks.title: P20.java

blocks.code:
$ java P20.java
a c -> true
d e f -> true
g h -> false calls=7
5
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`&&` binds tighter than `||`. In `f(a) && t(b) || t(c)`, `b` is skipped, then `c` runs. `|` and `&` always evaluate both operands, and `&` binds tighter than `|`, so `d | (e & f)` evaluates all three. In `r4`, `x > 3` is true so `x++` never runs and `x` stays `5`. `^` on booleans is exclusive or.

#### Puzzle 21. Switch fall-through (intermediate)

blocks.title: P21.java

blocks.code:
$ java P21.java
n=1: one two
n=2: two
n=3: three default four
n=4: four
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Old-style `case` labels fall through until a `break`. For `n=1`: `one`, then falls into `two`. For `n=3`: `three`, falls into `default`, falls into `case 4`: `default` position does not matter for matching (it is used only if nothing matches) but it matters for fall-through. Arrow cases (`case 1 ->`) never fall through, which is one reason to prefer them.

#### Puzzle 22. Pattern switch, guards and null (advanced)

blocks.title: P22.java

blocks.code:
$ java P22.java
int 5
big int 50
empty string
string 3
null!
other Double
old switch on null string: NPE
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Cases are tested top to bottom, so the guarded `Integer i when i > 10` must come before the plain `Integer i` (the other order is a compile error: dominance). `case null` is allowed in pattern switches since Java 21; without it a `null` selector throws a `NullPointerException`, which is still what the old string switch does.

### Numbers, operators and characters

#### Puzzle 23. Integer overflow (basic)

blocks.title: P23.java

blocks.text:
Integer arithmetic wraps around silently in two's complement. `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative because `+2147483648` does not fit. `(byte) 200` keeps the low 8 bits, giving `-56`. `1_000_000 * 1_000_000` is computed in `int` before any widening, so the result is wrong even though the target would hold it; make one operand `long`. The microsecond constant has the same bug: `24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000` overflows `int`. Use `Math.multiplyExact` when overflow is an error.

#### Puzzle 24. Floating point surprises (intermediate)

blocks.title: P24.java

blocks.code:
$ java P24.java
0.30000000000000004
true
false
false
false
true
true
false
Infinity
0
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3` in binary floating point. The `float` version accidentally rounds to the same `float` as `0.3f`, which shows that you cannot reason about equality by feel. `0.1f == 0.1` is `false` because the float is widened to a different double. `NaN` is not equal to itself with `==`, but `Double.equals` treats it as equal (so it works as a map key), and `0.0 == -0.0` is `true` while `Double.equals` says `false`. Casting `NaN` to `int` gives `0`.

#### Puzzle 25. Compound assignment and increments (intermediate)

blocks.title: P25.java

blocks.code:
$ java P25.java
54
2
12
3
5
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Compound assignment has a hidden cast: `b += 300` is `b = (byte)(b + 300)`, which wraps to `54`, and `s += 1.9` is `s =` `(short)(s + 1.9)`, truncating to `2`. For `i = i++ + ++i`: left operand evaluates to 5 (and `i` becomes 6), `++i` makes 7, sum 12. `j = j++` assigns the old value back, so `j` stays `3`. In `k += expr` the old value of `k` is saved before the right side runs: `1 + (1 + 3) = 5`. Do not write such expressions.

#### Puzzle 26. Rounding, division and remainder with negatives (intermediate)

blocks.title: P26.java

blocks.text:
`Math.round` rounds half up (towards positive infinity): `2.5` becomes `3`, `-2.5` becomes `-2`. A cast truncates towards zero (`-2.7` becomes `-2`), while `Math.floor` goes down. Integer division truncates towards zero, and `%` takes the sign of the dividend, so `-7 % 3 == -1` and `7 % -3 == 1`. `Math.floorMod` and `Math.floorDiv` give the mathematical (floor) versions, which is what you want for array wrap-around indices.

#### Puzzle 27. Division by zero and edge values (intermediate)

blocks.title: P27.java

blocks.code:
$ java P27.java
Infinity
-Infinity
NaN
NaN
/ by zero
/ by zero
true
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Integer division or remainder by zero throws `ArithmeticException: / by zero`. Floating point never throws: it yields `Infinity`, `-Infinity` or `NaN`. `Double.MIN_VALUE` is the smallest positive double, not the most negative one. `Integer.MIN_VALUE` equals its own negation because of overflow.

#### Puzzle 28. Shifts and literals (advanced)

blocks.title: P28.java

blocks.text:
Shift distances are masked to 5 bits for `int` (6 for `long`), so `1 << 32` is `1 << 0` and `1 << 33` is `2`. `>>` keeps the sign, `>>>` fills with zeros. A `byte` is promoted to `int` before shifting, so `b >>> 4` on `-16` shifts a 32-bit value and gives `268435455`; casting back to `byte` yields `-1`. A leading zero means octal (`010` is 8). `0xFFFFFFFF` is an `int` literal with value `-1`, widened to `long` as `-1`; write `0xFFFFFFFFL` for the large value.

#### Puzzle 29. Floating point in loops (intermediate)

blocks.title: P29.java

blocks.text:
Adding `0.1` ten times gives `0.9999999999999999`, so a loop with `d != 1.0` never ends (the code stops it with a counter). Always loop with an integer counter or use `<`. A `float` has 24 bits of mantissa: above 16,777,216 adding 1 changes nothing. Casting a too-large `double` to `long` saturates at `Long.MAX_VALUE` rather than wrapping.

#### Puzzle 30. char arithmetic and string concatenation (intermediate)

blocks.title: P30.java

blocks.code:
$ java P30.java
98
b
195
ab
195c
3x12
c
1
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`'a' + 1` is an `int` (98); cast back for the character. Two chars added are an `int` (195), unless a `String` is already on the left. Evaluation is left to right: `1 + 2 + "x" + 1 + 2` is `3x12`. Compound assignment and `++` on a `char` keep the type, so `c` ends as `c`. `new StringBuilder('a')` picks the `StringBuilder(int capacity)` constructor with capacity 97, not the text `a`, so the builder holds only `b`, length 1.

### Strings, arrays and collections

#### Puzzle 31. split surprises (intermediate)

blocks.title: P31.java

blocks.code:
$ java P31.java
2
2
1
[a, |, b]
[a, b]
0
4
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`split` removes trailing empty strings, but keeps a leading one: `"a,b,,"` gives 2, `",a"` gives 2. `"".split(",")` returns an array with one empty string. The argument is a regular expression, so `"|"` means an empty alternation that splits between every character, and `"."` matches everything, leaving only empty strings that are trimmed away (length 0). Escape with `\\|` or use `Pattern.quote`. A negative limit keeps trailing empties.

#### Puzzle 32. Mutable keys in a HashMap (intermediate)

blocks.title: P32.java

blocks.code:
$ java P32.java
null
null
false
1
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The entry was stored in the bucket for hash `1`. After `k.id = 2`, lookup with `k` goes to the bucket for hash 2 and finds nothing. A new `Key(1)` goes to the right bucket but the stored key is no longer equal to it. The entry is still in the map (size 1) but unreachable. Use immutable keys: records, strings, wrappers. Also note `"Aa"` and `"BB"` have equal hash codes: equal hashes do not imply equal objects.

#### Puzzle 33. equals without hashCode (intermediate)

blocks.title: P33.java

blocks.code:
$ java P33.java
2
true
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Two points that are `equals` land in different buckets because the inherited identity `hashCode` differs, so the set holds both and `contains` fails (almost always; a collision would be luck). The contract is: equal objects must have equal hash codes. Override both together, or use a record.

#### Puzzle 34. List.remove(int) versus remove(Object) (basic)

blocks.title: P34.java

blocks.text:
With `List<Integer>`, `remove(1)` picks the `remove(int index)` overload and removes the element at index 1 (`20`). To remove the value, box it explicitly: `Integer.valueOf(1)` or a cast to `Object`. Overload resolution prefers the primitive overload in phase 1.

#### Puzzle 35. Arrays.asList and List.of (intermediate)

blocks.title: P35.java

blocks.code:
$ java P35.java
Z
[Z, Y, c]
add: UnsupportedOperationException
List.of is immutable
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`Arrays.asList` returns a fixed-size list that is a view of the array: `set` writes through to the array, and changes to the array are visible in the list, but `add` and `remove` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `List.of` returns a truly immutable list, where even `set` throws. Wrap in `new ArrayList<>(...)` if you need an independent mutable copy.

#### Puzzle 36. Removing inside a for-each loop (advanced)

blocks.title: P36.java

blocks.code:
$ java P36.java
removing a -> CME
removing b -> [a, c]
removing c -> CME
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Removing from an `ArrayList` during iteration usually throws `ConcurrentModificationException`, but not always. `hasNext()` just compares the cursor with the size. After removing the second-to-last element, the cursor equals the new size, so the loop ends before `next()` can check the modification counter. Removing the first or last element does throw. Do not depend on this; use `Iterator.remove()` or `removeIf`.

#### Puzzle 37. Autoboxing in collection calls (advanced)

blocks.title: P37.java

blocks.code:
$ java P37.java
10
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`i - 1` is an `int`, so `set.remove(i - 1)` boxes to `Integer`, but the set contains `Short` objects. `Integer.equals(Short)` is always `false`, so nothing is ever removed and the size is `10`. The fix is `set.remove((short) (i - 1))`. `remove(Object)` takes any object, so the compiler cannot warn you.

#### Puzzle 38. Null keys, null values and Map methods (intermediate)

blocks.title: P38.java

blocks.code:
$ java P38.java
1 null null
true false
5
12
12 0
Map.of duplicate key
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`HashMap` permits one `null` key and `null` values, so `get` returning `null` cannot tell absence from a stored `null`: use `containsKey`. `putIfAbsent` treats a mapping to `null` as absent, so it stores `5`. `merge` combines with the existing value (`5` `+ 7`). `getOrDefault` only supplies a default when the key is missing. `Map.of` rejects duplicate keys and nulls.

#### Puzzle 39. BigDecimal equality (advanced)

blocks.title: P39.java

blocks.text:
`BigDecimal.equals` compares value and scale, so `2.0` and `2.00` are not equal, while `compareTo` ignores scale. `HashSet` uses `equals`/`hashCode` and keeps both; `TreeSet` uses `compareTo` and keeps one. Neither collection is wrong: they define "same" differently. `new BigDecimal(0.1)` shows the exact binary value of the double; `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)` uses the canonical string, which is what you nearly always want.

#### Puzzle 40. Subtraction comparators (advanced)

blocks.title: P40.java

blocks.text:
`(x, y) -> x - y` overflows when the operands are far apart: `5 - MIN_VALUE` is negative although 5 is larger, so the comparator is inconsistent and the sort result is garbage (and may even throw `Comparison method violates its` `general contract!` for larger inputs). Use `Integer.compare(x, y)` or `Comparator.naturalOrder()`. The wrong order shown is what this JDK printed; other inputs fail differently.

#### Puzzle 41. Arrays: covariance, aliasing and clone (intermediate)

blocks.title: P41.java

blocks.code:
$ java P41.java
ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer
99
null
5
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Arrays are covariant, so `Object[] objs = new String[1]` compiles, but the array remembers its real type and stores check it at run time: `ArrayStoreException`. Assigning an array copies the reference, so `a[0]` sees the change. A new `int[2][]` has `null` rows. `clone()` on a 2D array is shallow: the rows are shared, so `rows[0][0]` changes too.

### Generics, records, enums, lambdas, streams and threads

#### Puzzle 42. Type erasure and heap pollution (advanced)

blocks.title: P42.java

blocks.code:
$ java P42.java
true
1
ClassCastException at the use site
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Generic type arguments are erased, so at run time both lists are plain `ArrayList` and `getClass()` returns the same class. A raw-type cast lets an `Integer` into a `List<String>` without any error at that point. The failure appears later, at the compiler-inserted cast where the element is used as a `String`. This is the reason to avoid raw types and unchecked casts.

#### Puzzle 43. Record equality with arrays (intermediate)

blocks.title: P43.java

blocks.code:
$ java P43.java
true
false
true
Money[cents=5]
true
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
A record's `equals` compares components with `equals` (or `==` for primitives). An `int[]` component uses array identity, so two records holding equal-looking but different arrays are not equal, while records sharing the same array instance are. `Money` has only a primitive, so value equality works and `toString` is generated. Prefer `List` over arrays in records, or override `equals` and `hashCode`.

#### Puzzle 44. Enum basics (basic)

blocks.title: P44.java

blocks.code:
$ java P44.java
true
1 -1
No enum constant P44.Level.mid
class P44$Level class P44$Level
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Enum constants are singletons, so `==` is correct and null-safe. `valueOf` is case-sensitive and throws `IllegalArgumentException` for an unknown name. `compareTo` compares ordinals (`MID` is 1, `HIGH` is 2, difference -1). A constant without a body has the enum type as its class; a constant with a body would be an anonymous subclass, which is why `getDeclaringClass()` exists.

#### Puzzle 45. What a lambda captures (intermediate)

blocks.title: P45.java

blocks.code:
$ java P45.java
0 10 20
3
after / lambda sees a copy of the value
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
A lambda captures the value of local variables, which must be effectively final. The loop variable `i` is not effectively final, so the code copies it to `copy` first, and each lambda has its own value. To accumulate state, the usual trick is a one-element array (or `AtomicInteger`), because the variable is final but its content is not. Reassigning `text` afterwards is fine here only because the lambda did not capture it.

#### Puzzle 46. Java is always pass by value (basic)

blocks.title: P46.java

blocks.code:
$ java P46.java
1 99 sb! s
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The method receives copies of the values: copies of the primitive and of the references. Mutating through the copy of a reference (`arr[0] = 99`, `sb.append`) changes the shared object, while reassigning the parameter (`arr = new` `int[]...`, `sb = new...`, `s = s + "!"`) only changes the local copy. Strings are immutable, so the caller's `s` can never change.

#### Puzzle 47. orElse versus orElseGet (intermediate)

blocks.title: P47.java

blocks.code:
$ java P47.java
computing for orElse
value
value
computing for empty
default
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The argument of `orElse` is an ordinary expression and is always evaluated, even when the `Optional` has a value. `orElseGet` takes a supplier that runs only when needed. Use `orElseGet` when the default is expensive or has side effects.

#### Puzzle 48. Lazy streams and element-wise processing (intermediate)

blocks.title: P48.java

blocks.code:
$ java P48.java
no terminal operation yet
filter a
map a
got A
filter b
map b
got B
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Intermediate operations only describe the pipeline; with no terminal operation nothing runs, so `peek` printed nothing. Elements flow through the whole pipeline one at a time (filter, map, forEach for `a`, then for `b`), not stage by stage. `limit(2)` stops the pipeline after two elements, so `c` is never touched. This laziness is also why side effects in stream stages are a bad idea.

#### Puzzle 49. Streams are single use (basic)

blocks.title: P49.java

blocks.code:
$ java P49.java
2
stream has already been operated upon or closed
[3, 1, 2]
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
A stream can be consumed once; the second terminal operation throws `IllegalStateException`. Stream operations never modify the source collection: `sorted()` sorts a temporary copy and the list stays `[3, 1, 2]`.

#### Puzzle 50. run versus start (intermediate)

blocks.title: P50.java

blocks.code:
$ java P50.java
in main
in worker
cannot restart: TERMINATED
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Calling `run()` just calls the method on the current thread, which is why it prints `main`. `start()` creates a new thread that executes `run()`. A thread can be started only once; a second `start` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`, and the thread state is `TERMINATED` after it finishes.

### Patterns behind the puzzles

Looking back, almost every puzzle falls into one of a handful of families. Learning the families is faster than memorising fifty answers.

rows: `==` compares references for objects; caches and constant folding make some of them true
operands left to right, `&&` and `||` short-circuit, `&` and `|` do not
only instance methods are virtual; overloads are chosen at compile time
operands widen to `int` at least; compound assignment casts back silently
equals and hashCode together; comparators must be consistent
streams and `orElseGet` defer work until needed
blocks.caption: Families of puzzles and the rule behind each.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Use these ideas in every output question.

- Name the rule: constant folding, cache range, most specific overload, short-circuit, numeric promotion.
- Reference types compare with `equals`; `==` on boxes and strings is only identity.
- Static initialisers run once per class, instance initialisers once per object, super before sub.
- Only instance methods dispatch dynamically; fields, statics and private methods do not.
- Compound assignment and narrowing casts hide overflow; use `Math.xxxExact` where it matters.
- Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and comparators must never overflow.

Coding rounds reward a repeatable method more than memorised answers. For every problem in this chapter we follow the same loop: restate the problem with one example, state the brute-force solution and its cost, ask what work is repeated or wasted, then write the improved version and say its time and space complexity. Say these steps out loud in an interview; the interviewer is grading your thinking as much as your code.

Every solution below was compiled and run on OpenJDK 21. The listings are static methods of one class, `Ch7`, and the driver at the end of the chapter calls all of them on small sample inputs. Complexities use n for the input length. Strings and arrays are the bread and butter of first-round interviews because they test loops, indices and edge cases without needing a library.

### The method, in five steps

1. **Clarify.** Ask about empty input, null, duplicates, negative numbers, case sensitivity, and size limits. "Can the array be empty?" is a good question; a wrong assumption costs more than the ten seconds it takes to ask.
2. **Brute force.** State the obvious O(n^2) or O(n^3) approach first. It proves you understand the problem and gives you a correctness oracle.
3. **Find the waste.** Which work repeats? A nested loop that recomputes a sum suggests a running sum; a nested loop that looks for a match suggests a hash set or sorting; a window that restarts suggests two pointers.
4. **Code it cleanly.** Small methods, meaningful names, no clever one-liners.
5. **Test by hand.** Walk one normal case and two edge cases (empty, single element) through your code before saying "done".

rows: pair in sorted data, palindromes, in-place filtering
longest or shortest contiguous range with a property
best subarray, best buy and sell

blocks.text:
### String problems

#### Problem 1. Reverse a string and the words of a sentence (basic)

Reversing characters is a two-pointer swap on a `char[]`. Reversing the order of words splits on runs of whitespace and walks the pieces backwards; `trim` plus `split("\\s+")` handles leading, trailing and repeated spaces.

blocks.title: Reversal

blocks.text:
Both run in O(n) time. The character reversal needs O(n) extra space for the array copy because `String` is immutable; `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()` does the same in one line, and you may say so, but be ready to write the loop.

#### Problem 2. Valid palindrome ignoring punctuation (basic)

Two pointers start at the ends and move inward, skipping characters that are not letters or digits. No cleaned copy of the string is built, so the space is O(1).

blocks.title: Palindrome

blocks.text:
Notice the inner `i < j` guards: without them a string made only of punctuation would run the pointers off the ends.

#### Problem 3. Valid anagram (basic)

Two strings are anagrams when every letter occurs equally often in both. Sorting both gives O(n log n); a counting array gives O(n) time and O(1) space (26 counters). One array is enough: add for the first string, subtract for the second, and check that all counters return to zero.

blocks.title: Anagram

blocks.text:
This version assumes lowercase `a` to `z`. For arbitrary Unicode, replace the array with a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` (or `int[65536]` for the Basic Multilingual Plane).

#### Problem 4. First non-repeating character (basic)

Two passes: count every character, then scan the string in order and return the first index whose count is one. Two passes beat the brute-force "for each character scan the rest" (O(n^2)).

blocks.title: FirstUnique

blocks.text:
#### Problem 5. Longest substring without repeating characters (intermediate)

The brute force tries every start and extends until a repeat appears: O(n^2). The waste is that after a repeat at position j we throw the window away and rebuild it. A **sliding window** keeps two indices, `start` and `end`, and a table of where each character was last seen. When the new character was seen inside the current window, `start` jumps to just past that earlier occurrence.

blocks.title: NoRepeat

blocks.text:
The condition `lastSeen[c] >= start` matters. A character seen before the window began is not a conflict; without the comparison, input such as `abba` would drag `start` backwards. Each index moves forward only, so the time is O(n); space is O(alphabet).

#### Problem 6. Run-length compression (basic)

Walk the string, count runs of equal characters, and emit character-plus-count. The loop runs to `i <= length` so the last run is flushed by the same code path as the others. Return the original if the "compressed" form is not shorter.

blocks.title: Compress

blocks.text:
Building with `StringBuilder` keeps this O(n); concatenating with `+=` in the loop would be O(n^2) because each concatenation copies.

#### Problem 7. Longest common prefix (basic)

Start with the first word as the candidate prefix and shorten it until every word starts with it. Worst case O(total characters).

blocks.title: Prefix

blocks.text:
#### Problem 8. Longest palindromic substring (intermediate)

A palindrome mirrors around its centre. There are 2n-1 centres (n characters plus n-1 gaps), and expanding outward from each costs O(n), so the whole search is O(n^2) time and O(1) space. A brute force that tests every substring is O(n^3). Dynamic programming also gives O(n^2) but needs O(n^2) memory, so expansion is the better interview answer. (Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n) but is rarely expected.)

blocks.title: LongestPalindrome

blocks.text:
For `babad` both `bab` and `aba` are valid; the strict `>` keeps the first one found. State that tie-breaking rule out loud.

### Array problems

#### Problem 9. Move zeroes to the end, keeping order (basic)

Keep a `write` index marking where the next non-zero belongs, and swap each non-zero element into it. One pass, in place, O(n) time and O(1) space. Swapping (rather than copying and then zero-filling) keeps the loop to a single pass.

blocks.title: MoveZeroes

blocks.text:
#### Problem 10. Rotate an array right by k (intermediate)

The easy answer copies into a new array at `(i + k) % n`: O(n) time, O(n) space. The in-place trick is three reversals: reverse everything, then reverse the first k elements, then the remaining n-k. For `[1..7]` and k = 3: reversing all gives `7 6 5 4 3 2 1`; reversing the first three gives `5 6 7 4 3 2 1`; reversing the last four gives `5 6 7 1 2 3 4`.

blocks.title: Rotate

blocks.text:
The `k %= a.length` line handles k larger than n. Rotating an empty array would divide by zero, so guard it if empty input is allowed.

#### Problem 11. Maximum subarray sum (intermediate)

Brute force sums every subarray: O(n^2) with a running sum (O(n^3) if you recompute sums). **Kadane's algorithm** asks, at each element, "is it better to extend the best subarray ending at the previous element, or to start fresh here?" That is one comparison per element.

blocks.title: MaxSubarray

blocks.text:
Initialise from `a[0]`, not from 0, or an all-negative array wrongly returns 0 (for `{-3, -1, -2}` the right answer is `-1`).

#### Problem 12. Best time to buy and sell a stock once (basic)

Brute force tries every buy/sell pair, O(n^2). The waste is looking backwards repeatedly: the best buy day for any sell day is simply the minimum price so far. Track it while scanning.

blocks.title: Stock

blocks.text:
Starting `best` at 0 means "do not trade" is a valid answer, which is why the descending prices case returns 0.

#### Problem 13. Missing number in 0..n (basic)

An array of n distinct numbers drawn from 0..n has exactly one value missing. Sum formula (`n(n+1)/2` minus the actual sum) works but the sum can overflow for large n. XOR is safe: `x ^ x == 0`, so XOR-ing every index and every value cancels all pairs and leaves the missing value.

blocks.title: Missing

blocks.text:
#### Problem 14. Product of array except self (intermediate)

The brute force multiplies the other n-1 elements for each position: O(n^2). Dividing the total product by `a[i]` fails when the array contains zeros (and the question usually forbids division). The fix is two sweeps: the left sweep stores the product of everything to the left in `out[i]`, and the right sweep multiplies in the product of everything to the right using a single running variable.

blocks.title: Product

blocks.text:
Time O(n), extra space O(1) beyond the output array. Watch for `int` overflow if the values are large; use `long` or `BigInteger` if the constraints demand it.

#### Problem 15. Binary search, and the overflow bug (basic)

On sorted data, halve the range each step: O(log n). The classic bug is `mid = (lo + hi) / 2`, which overflows `int` when the sum exceeds 2,147,483,647. That bug sat in the JDK's own `Arrays.binarySearch` and in many textbooks for years; `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is safe. Returning `-(lo + 1)` for a miss matches `Arrays.binarySearch`: the negative value encodes the insertion point.

blocks.title: BinarySearch

blocks.text:
#### Problem 16. Majority element (intermediate)

A majority element appears more than n/2 times. A `HashMap` of counts is O(n) time and O(n) space. **Boyer-Moore** **voting** does it in O(1) space: keep a candidate and a vote count; matching elements add a vote, others cancel one, and when the votes hit zero the next element becomes the candidate. Because the majority element outnumbers everything else combined, it survives all the cancellations.

blocks.title: Majority

blocks.text:
If a majority is not guaranteed you need a second pass to verify the candidate.

blocks.text: Every line matches the expected answer for the sample input: for instance 6 is the best subarray `4, -1, 2, 1`, and 5 is the best profit (buy at 1, sell at 6).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you pick the right technique when you see a new array or string problem? Look at what is being asked. "Contiguous range with a property" points to a sliding window or a running value (Kadane). "Pairs or ends" in sorted or palindromic data points to two pointers. "Count or compare letters" points to a frequency array. "Everything except me" points to prefix and suffix passes. If none applies, state the brute force, then ask which work it repeats; the answer usually names the technique.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Test edge cases before the interviewer asks: empty input, one element, all equal, all negative, already sorted. Most "it passed my example" bugs live in those five.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Strings and arrays problems are solved by a few reusable patterns:

- Always state the brute force and its cost first, then name the repeated work you are removing.
- Two pointers, sliding windows and running values (Kadane, minimum so far) turn nested loops into one pass.
- Frequency arrays and hash maps trade O(alphabet) or O(n) space for linear time.
- Prefix/suffix passes and reversal tricks give O(1) extra space for "everything except me" and rotation.
- Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, initialise from the first element, and test empty, single and all-negative inputs.

sections.title: Coding Problems: Collections, Recursion and Dynamic Programming

blocks.text:
### Programming

The second family of coding problems is about choosing the right data structure and the right way to break a problem into smaller copies of itself. A `HashMap` turns a nested loop into a lookup; a `Deque` turns nested brackets into a stack; recursion with backtracking enumerates choices; dynamic programming (DP) remembers sub-answers so that they are computed once. All solutions here compile and run on OpenJDK 21; the driver and its real output close the chapter. The listings are members of one class, `Ch8`.

### Hash maps, stacks, heaps and sorting

#### Problem 1. Two sum (basic)

Given an array and a target, return the indices of two numbers adding up to it. Brute force checks every pair: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. The waste is searching for the partner by scanning. Store each value's index in a `HashMap` as you go, and for each element look up `target - value` in O(1): O(n) time, O(n) space. One pass is enough because the partner is either already seen (found now) or will find this element later.

blocks.title: TwoSum

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2. Contains duplicate (basic)

`HashSet.add` returns `false` when the element is already present, so insertion doubles as the test. O(n) time, O(n) space; sorting first and comparing neighbours is O(n log n) time with no extra set.

blocks.title: Duplicates

blocks.text:
#### Problem 3. Group anagrams (intermediate)

All anagrams share one **canonical key**: the word with its letters sorted. Use that key in a map from key to list of words. Sorting each word costs O(k log k) for word length k, so the total is O(n k log k). `LinkedHashMap` keeps groups in first-seen order, which makes the output deterministic.

blocks.title: GroupAnagrams

blocks.text:
`computeIfAbsent` creates the list only for the first word of each group. A faster key for lowercase words is a 26-element count array turned into a string, giving O(n k).

#### Problem 4. Top K frequent words (intermediate)

Count with `merge`, then pick the k largest counts. Sorting all distinct words costs O(m log m) for m distinct words. A **min-heap of size k** costs O(m log k): offer every entry, and whenever the heap grows past k, `poll` removes the weakest. The comparator puts lower counts first and, for equal counts, the alphabetically later word first, so that ties resolve toward the alphabetically smaller word.

blocks.title: TopK

blocks.text:
This is the standard use of `PriorityQueue`: the heap is a min-heap, so to keep the k largest you evict the smallest.

#### Problem 5. Balanced brackets (basic)

A stack matches the most recent opener with each closer. The trick that keeps the code short is to push the closer you expect, so the check on a closing bracket is a single comparison. Use `ArrayDeque` as the stack; `java.util.Stack` is a legacy synchronised class. O(n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.title: Brackets

blocks.text:
Two failure cases must be handled: a closer arriving on an empty stack (`)(`), and leftover openers at the end (`((`).

#### Problem 6. Merge intervals (intermediate)

Sort by start. Then one sweep: if the next interval starts after the last output interval ends, there is a gap and it begins a new interval; otherwise they overlap and the last interval's end is extended to the larger of the two ends. Sorting dominates: O(n log n).

blocks.title: MergeIntervals

blocks.text:
Remember `Math.max` when extending: `[1, 10]` followed by `[2, 3]` must keep the end at 10.

#### Problem 7. LRU cache (intermediate)

A least-recently-used cache evicts the entry that has gone unused longest. In Java the shortest correct answer is `LinkedHashMap` in **access-order** mode, with `removeEldestEntry` overridden to evict when the size passes the capacity. `get` and `put` are O(1).

blocks.title: LruCache

blocks.text: Interviewers often ask for it without `LinkedHashMap`. The classic structure is a hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency, with sentinel head and tail nodes so that inserting and unlinking never need null checks.

blocks.title: ManualLru

blocks.text:
`LinkedHashMap` is the same design built into the JDK. Neither version is thread-safe; wrap with `Collections.synchronizedMap` or use a library such as Caffeine in production.

### Recursion and backtracking

#### Problem 8. All permutations (intermediate)

**Backtracking** builds a candidate step by step: choose, explore, un-choose. The `used` array records which elements are in the current permutation; when the permutation is complete, add a *copy* of it to the result (adding `cur` itself would store the same list n! times, which then ends up empty). There are n! results, so the time is O(n \* n!).

blocks.title: Permutations

blocks.text:
#### Problem 9. All subsets (basic)

The iterative form is neat: start with the empty subset; for each element, copy every existing subset and add the element to the copy. The count doubles each time, so the result has 2^n subsets and the work is O(n \* 2^n).

blocks.title: Subsets

blocks.text:
### Graph search on grids and trees

#### Problem 10. Number of islands (intermediate)

In a grid of `1` (land) and `0` (water), count connected groups of land. Scan the grid; on meeting unvisited land, count one island and run a **depth-first search** that flips every connected land cell to water so it is never counted again. O(rows \* cols) time. The recursion depth can reach the number of cells, so for very large grids use an explicit stack or BFS to avoid `StackOverflowError`.

blocks.title: Islands

blocks.text:
#### Problem 11. Shortest path in a maze (intermediate)

When every step costs the same, **breadth-first search** (BFS) finds the shortest path, because it visits cells in order of distance. Use a queue and a distance table that doubles as the visited set. O(rows \* cols).

blocks.title: ShortestPath

blocks.text:
DFS goes deep first and uses a stack (or recursion); BFS goes level by level and uses a queue. For shortest paths in unweighted graphs, choose BFS; for weighted graphs use Dijkstra.

#### Problem 12. Level-order traversal of a binary tree (basic)

BFS on a tree. The inner loop runs exactly `queue.size()` times, which is the number of nodes on the current level, so each level lands in its own list. A recursive `height` shows the other natural style: the answer for a node is built from the answers of its children.

blocks.title: LevelOrder

blocks.text:
### Dynamic programming basics

DP applies when a problem has **overlapping subproblems** (the same sub-question recurs) and **optimal** **substructure** (the best answer is built from best answers of the parts). The recipe: define what `dp[i]` means in words, write the recurrence, fix the base case, and choose the evaluation order. Top-down (recursion plus a memo table) and bottom-up (a loop filling a table) give the same answer.

#### Problem 13. Fibonacci in three costs (basic)

The naive recursion recomputes the same values and takes O(2^n) time. Memoising each result brings it to O(n). The bottom-up loop needs only the last two values: O(n) time, O(1) space. `long` overflows at `fib(93)`, which is why the driver stops at 90.

blocks.title: Fibonacci

blocks.text:
The climbing-stairs problem (one or two steps at a time) is the same recurrence with different base cases.

#### Problem 14. Coin change, fewest coins (intermediate)

`dp[a]` is the fewest coins that make amount `a`. For each coin that fits, `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1)`. Starting every cell at `amount + 1` acts as infinity without risking overflow. Time O(amount \* coins), space O(amount). A greedy "take the largest coin" fails: for coins 1, 5, 11 and amount 15 greedy picks 11 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 (five coins) while the best is 5 + 5 + 5.

blocks.title: CoinChange

blocks.text:
#### Problem 15. Longest common subsequence (intermediate)

`dp[i][j]` is the LCS length of the first i characters of `a` and the first j of `b`. If the last characters match, extend the diagonal; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string. O(n \* m) time and space; keeping only two rows reduces space to O(min(n, m)) when you need just the length.

blocks.title: Lcs

blocks.text:
#### Problem 16. 0/1 knapsack (intermediate)

Each item can be taken once. `dp[w]` is the best value achievable with capacity `w`. The detail interviewers probe is the loop direction: iterating `w` **downwards** guarantees each item is considered at most once, because `dp[w - weight]` still holds the value from before this item. Iterating upwards would let an item be reused, which solves the *unbounded* knapsack instead.

blocks.title: Knapsack

blocks.text: ### Running all the solutions

blocks.title: Ch8.java (driver, inside main)

blocks.text: Check a few by hand: the best coin change for 15 is 3 coins; the LCS of `ABCBDAB` and `BDCABA` is 4; the knapsack picks the items of weight 3 and 4 for value 9; and the maze path of length 6 goes down, right along the bottom row, then up to `E`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When do you use DP instead of plain recursion? When the recursion tree contains the same subproblem many times (overlapping subproblems) and the best answer for a problem can be assembled from best answers to its parts. Naive Fibonacci is the textbook example: 2^n calls but only n distinct inputs. Add a memo table (top-down) or fill a table in dependency order (bottom-up) and the time drops to the number of distinct states times the work per state.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: In backtracking, `out.add(cur)` stores a reference to a list that you keep mutating. Always add `new ArrayList<>(cur)`. The symptom is a result full of identical (often empty) lists.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Collections and DP problems come down to choosing state and structure:

- A `HashMap` or `HashSet` replaces an inner search loop; a `Deque` is the stack or queue; a `PriorityQueue` of size k solves top-k in O(n log k).
- Backtracking is choose, explore, un-choose, and results must be copies.
- BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS counts or explores components.
- DP needs a clear meaning for each state, a recurrence and a base case; loop direction matters (knapsack).
- `LinkedHashMap` with access order and `removeEldestEntry` is a complete LRU cache; know the hand-written list-plus-map design too.

Concurrency questions in interviews rarely ask you to recite the Java Memory Model. They ask you to write a small, correct, thread-safe program on a whiteboard: "print odd and even numbers from two threads in order", "implement a producer-consumer", "fix this deadlock". This chapter gives eight such tasks. Each has the problem, the idea, a complete solution and the real output of running it on OpenJDK 21. The listings are members of one class, `Ch9`, and a single driver at the end runs them all. For the theory behind the tools used here (monitors, `volatile`, the executors) see the concurrency Part earlier in the book.

### Tools you will reach for

Before writing code, decide which of these a task needs. Choosing the tool is most of the answer.

rows: one global lock order, or `tryLock` with timeout
blocks.caption: Concurrency tools and when to choose them.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never create threads with `new Thread` in production code for task-style work; use an `ExecutorService`. The solutions below use raw threads in two tasks only because the task is *about* thread coordination.

### Task 1. Print odd and even numbers alternately with two threads

One thread prints odd numbers, the other even numbers, and the output must interleave in order. The shared state is the next number to print. A thread whose turn it is not waits on the monitor; after printing it calls `notifyAll` so the partner re-checks its condition. The `wait` call is always inside a `while` loop that re-tests the condition, because of spurious wakeups and because `notifyAll` wakes every waiter.

blocks.title: OddEven

blocks.text:
What to notice: all reads and writes of `next` happen while holding `lock`; the final `notifyAll` after the loop frees a partner that is still waiting when the last number has been printed. Without it one thread can wait forever, a hang you only see about once in a hundred runs. A `Semaphore` pair (each thread releases the other's permit) is an equally good answer.

### Task 2. Producer-consumer with a bounded queue

A producer creates items faster than a consumer processes them. A bounded `BlockingQueue` solves two problems at once: `put` blocks when the queue is full (back-pressure, so memory stays bounded) and `take` blocks when it is empty (no busy-waiting). A **poison pill**, a special value, tells the consumer to stop.

blocks.title: ProducerConsumer

blocks.text:
Handling `InterruptedException` by restoring the interrupt flag (`Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`) is the correct habit; swallowing it hides shutdown requests. With several consumers you need one poison pill per consumer.

### Task 3. Create a deadlock, then fix it

Two threads each need two locks. Thread 1 takes A then B; thread 2 takes B then A. If each grabs its first lock before the other grabs its second, both wait forever. That is the four-part deadlock condition (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, **circular wait**). Break any one and it disappears; the cheapest to break is circular wait by giving all locks a global order.

blocks.title: Deadlock

blocks.text: The `sleepQuietly(50)` calls only make the bad interleaving certain for the demo. The good version orders locks by account id, so both threads lock account 1 before account 2 whichever direction the money flows. An alternative that avoids ordering is `tryLock(timeout)` on the second lock, releasing the first and retrying on failure. The driver starts each pair as daemon threads, waits half a second, and reports how many are still stuck; for the bad version the JVM itself can name them through `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` (the same information `jstack` prints as "Found one Java-level deadlock").

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you prevent and detect deadlocks? Prevent: acquire locks in a single global order, hold locks for as short a time as possible, never call unknown code (callbacks, overridable methods) while holding a lock, or use `tryLock` with a timeout. Detect: `jstack <pid>` or `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` lists Java-level deadlocks, and `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` does it programmatically.

### Task 4. A thread-safe counter

`count++` is three steps (read, add, write), so two threads can both read 5 and both write 6. The experiment below runs four threads, each incrementing four counters 100,000 times: a plain `int`, a `synchronized` method, an `AtomicInteger` and a `LongAdder`.

blocks.title: Counters

blocks.text:
The plain counter loses updates; the other three always reach exactly 400,000. `AtomicInteger` uses a hardware compare-and-set loop. `LongAdder` spreads contention over several cells and adds them up in `sum()`, which wins under heavy contention but is only a snapshot while writers run. Use `synchronized` when the counter must change together with other fields (an invariant spanning several variables), atomics for a single independent counter.

### Task 5. A thread-safe cache

`computeIfAbsent` on a `ConcurrentHashMap` is atomic for the key: if many threads ask for the same missing key, the loader runs once and the others wait for the value. The check-then-act version (`if (!map.containsKey(k))` `map.put(k, load(k))`) is not atomic and may load the same key repeatedly.

blocks.title: Cache

blocks.text:
Keep the loader short and never let it touch the same map: `computeIfAbsent` holds an internal lock on the bin while the loader runs, and a loader that updates the map can deadlock or throw. If loading is slow, cache a `CompletableFuture<V>` instead.

### Task 6. A thread-safe singleton

Three correct answers. The **holder idiom** relies on the JVM's class initialisation guarantee: `Holder` is initialised once, lazily, under the class-init lock, so no explicit synchronisation is needed. The **enum singleton** is the simplest and is also safe against serialization and reflection attacks. **Double-checked locking** works only if the field is `volatile`; mention it, but prefer the first two.

blocks.title: Singleton

blocks.text:
### Task 7. A rate limiter (token bucket)

Allow bursts up to `capacity` requests and a sustained `refillPerSecond`. State: the number of tokens and the time of the last refill. On each request, add the tokens earned since last time (capped at capacity), then spend one if at least one is available. The class takes the clock as a `LongSupplier` so a test can control time instead of sleeping.

blocks.title: TokenBucket

blocks.text:
All state changes happen in one `synchronized` method, so refilling and spending are a single atomic step. For a distributed system the same logic lives in a shared store such as Redis; libraries like Bucket4j or Resilience4j provide production versions.

### Task 8. Parallel sum

Sum a large array using several threads. Three styles are shown: manual chunks submitted to a fixed pool (the pool lives only for the call and is shut down in `finally`), a `RecursiveTask` that splits until the pieces are small, and a parallel stream.

blocks.title: ParallelSum

blocks.text:
Parallelism pays only when the work per element is large enough to outweigh splitting and thread hand-off. Summing a million numbers is so cheap that the sequential loop is typically as fast or faster; this task is about the structure, and you should say so in an interview.
